div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPTES.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPTES.
A high post—News by carrier-pigeon. THE autocrat of the breakfast table—The cook.

WATTS: "I don't believe women have any sense of humour at all." Potts: "My wife has. There can't anything happen out of the common but she says, Why, that's funny." FOR THE GOOD OF HUMANITY.—" Do you know a good tonic for nervous persons, Simpkins ?" "No ; what I want to find is a good tonic for people who have to live with them.' "PERFECT HAPPINESS," declared Aunt Sarah, "consists in &posing yourself the envy of all your friends." THERE is a good deal of satisfaction to be derived from deceiving people who think they are deceiving you. THE JUDGE: "What made you so certain that you had the right of way ? " The Driver: "Sure an' my waggon was the heaviest, yer honour."

_ BROWN : I'd like to see that new device of yours for preventing the theft of a watch. Jones: Can't show it. It was stolen from me yesterday by a pickpocket. WHERE SHE COMES IN. Finnicus : "I tell you a man never appreciates his wife till he gets into trouble." Cynnicus : " That's so; it's a big satisfaction to have some one to blame for HARDLY A SAFE PRECAUTION.—Husband (gently, to his wife, who is recovering from brain fever) : "You know, dear the doctor says you mustn't talk; so for a day or two just ask questions." ETHEL : "What kind of a man is this Mr. Rushington you speak of so often?" Jack: "Well, be is what we men call a good fellow." Ethel: "Mercy ! As bad as that?" THE rich are miserable because they have dis- covered that money cannot buy happiness, and the poor are wretched because they have not money enough to make the experiment. "YOUNG MAN," said the elderly gentleman in a choking voice, "she is the only daughter I have." "Yes," acknowledged the young man; that is one reason I thought I would like to marry her." FINANCIAL.—There isn't perfect confidence be- tween a man and his wife unless he voluntarily tells her when he has had his salary raised. HOSTESS: "I hope you found the bed comfort- able, Mr. Jenkins ? ' Jenkins: • "Excellent, madam! I nearly fell asleep in it." BIGGS : "How is your wife, old fellow. I heard she was indisposed?" Iliggi "Oh, she can't com- plain." 13i,Ns : "Dear me, is she as bad as that?" "WERE those cough-drops beneficial ?" "They worked like a charm. They have such a horrible taste that the children have all stopped coughing. Miss ANTIQUE—" Oh! I have had such a fright I was coming through that lonely wood, and I saw a man. I did run !" Miss Fritters—" Did you catch him?"

----- TREY were talking about dogs, "Well," said Snaggs. "I think many dogs have more sense than their masters." "Yes,' chimed in Craggs, "I have a dog like that myself." And he couldn't snake out why they laughed. JOHNNIE'S EVIDENCE. —Johnnie : "Ma, do they ever put fish in bottles?" Ma: "Not that I know of, my boy. What makes you ask ?" Johnnie: "Nothing; only I heard papa say that he had four bottles of Bass for dinner to-day."
THEIR FIP.ST BREAKFAST. Mr. Youngwed : "Darling, this egg seems to be pretty well cooked." Mrs. Youngwed (delighted): I thought so. Why, dearest, I boiled it for over half an hour."

THE HUSBAND'S OPPORTUNITY.— Mrs. Peck— "lf I had my life to go over again, I wouldn't marry the best man alive." Mr. H. Peck (his chance at last)—" You bet you wouldn't. I wouldn't ask you to." HE (just introduced) : "What a very homely person that gentleman near the piano is, Mrs. Black 1" She: "Isn't he ! That is Mr. Black." "How true it is, Mrs. Black, that the homely men always get the prettiest of wives !" RECIPROCITY.—A. : "When he was courting her he promised to throw everything at her feet." B.: "And did she reciprocate ? " "Well, I should rather say she did! After they were married she threw everything at his head." A POSSIBLE TRIUMPH.—Sam: " Dat ole preachah hab got de notion dat de world am gwine to run inter de sun next month an' git burned up." Bill: "I doan't take no stock in sech t'ings happenin'." Sam: "Well, if it do happen, he'll hab de laugh on us!" SOME SATTsFAcTiorr. Mrs. Bridewell : "I'm glad I wasn't born in France. Just think of hav- ing your husband selected for you by somebody else !" Mrs. Oldham: "I know; but there's the consolation of having somebody to blame after- wards." AMICABLY ARRANGED. —Jones : "I hear that the Smith family came to an amicable settlement about the distribution of the estate." Robinson: " Yes ; they agreed to divide the money equally, and they haven't spoken to one another since."

MERELY PREOAUTIONART.—Skinner : "Morton is a queer fellow. Did you ever notice that he never takes his eyes off you when you're talking to him?" Binner "Don't know that I ever did. Perhaps he isn't that way with everybody." "1 suppose you don't believe in courtship," said the paragraphist, laughingly, to the president of the gas company. "Why not?" asked the president. "Because lovers always turn the gas down, you know, Ha Ha 1 Ha 1" "Oh, that makes no difference," said the president. "The meter gets in its work all the same.' A HINDRANCE TO COURTSHIP.—Mr. Hilow : "I hear that Miss Munn, whom you call upon so frequently, is quite wealthy in her own right." Mr. Hudson: "So I hear." Mr. Hilow : "Any encumbrances?" Mr. Hudson: "A seven-year-old brother."

A MAN started in the livery stable business the other week, and the first thing he did was to have a big sign painted representing himself holding a mule by the bridle. "Is that a good likeness of me ? " he asked of an inquiring friend. "Yes—it is a perfect picture of you ; but who is the fellow holding you by the bridle ? " DRESSING HIM DOWN.—" I believe you'd stand before a mirror all day," said Mr. Closely, snap. pishly, "doing nothing but change your dresses." "Perhaps I would," replied Mrs. Closely, dreamily, " if I had the dresses.'

NOT AN EXPENSIVE LUXURY. - Mother (in horror) : "0, John I Don't you see what baby is doing? He is sucking all the paint off that monkey on the stick I" Father (deep in his paper) : "Oh, that's all right It only cost two cents. Don't be miserly, Mary!" PROVISION FOR BOTH. —Smith walked up Market- street the other evening with a box of chocolate under one arm and a big package of meat under the other. "Hello, Smith " said Brown ; "gone to housekeeping ? I didn't know you were married." "I'm not yet." "What are you doing with that chocolate and meat, then ?" "Going to see my girl." "Do you have to furnish the family with meat, already ? " "Oh, no; the chocolate is for the girl and the meat is for the dog. I have to square myself with both." MUCH PLEASANTER.—HOW much pleasanter it is to swing in a hammock and watch a man struggling with a lawn mower, and think how much pleasanter it is to swing in a hammock and watch a man struggling with a lawn mower, than it is to struggle with a lawn mower and think how much pleasanter it is to swing in a hammock and watch a man struggling with a lawn mower than it is to struggle with a lawn mower. The poor girl was so pleaied. I don't see how you men can be so untruthful." "I should think you'd know by this time that I'm never untruthful," said Mr. Coddington, reproachfully. "I said she was just as pretty as the could be, and so she was. "Thus philtre," said the wizard, "is guaranteed to make you happy for life. You will have everything heart can wish, and will be very happy." The lady smiled rapturously. " Splendid ! " she exclaimed, enthusiastically. " Splendid ! Just let me have a dozen bottles of that, please."

div.head: LADIFS' LErrk.at.
div.p: LADIFS' LErrk.at.

MY DEAR NMI" How delightfully fine and summer-like the weather is now becoming, and what a nice con- trast to that of a few weeks ago. The country begins to look at its best, and although perhaps it is rather early we may soon be looking forward to that delightful form of enjoyment, viz., picnics. In many places, I might say all places, there are particular spots dear to the picnic-party. Those who are fortunate enough to live by the side of a nice river may often have a most enjoyable time on its waters. But do not by any means think those who live away from the water cannot equally enjoy themselves, They can, for they make up for it in another way. I have often seen a party going in a small waggonette to some sylvan retreat any distance up to twelve miles away. But let me caution you against catching cold at night. For this purpose provide yourself with a cloak or a jacket. A friend of mine showed me her blouse which she purposed wearing at the next outing. The full vest was of pale blue silk and a cravat of creamy lace appeared at the throat. The waistband was of folded blue silk. Another friend, who was looking forward to the same event, was going to wear a plain white flannel with pale-coloured trimmings.

Let me now for a few minutes dilate upon the beauties of up-to-date millinery. The rage seems now to be for tufts of flowers, and they are ar- ranged with so much simplicity that they cannot help but charm the heart of any tasteful girl. They are of all varieties. Amongst those which I have seen recently are bunches of daisies lilies of the valley, pompom roses, and wall-flowers. They are for the most part dropped, as it were, on the rounded rustic straw. A favourite model is of brown straw, plain or bronzed, very silky-looking and light and plaited in fancy matting pattern. The crown is round, the brim wide and fiat without lining. Enormous shaded roses, iris or orchids are scattered over these hats, and secured with a knot of reeds. A black and white crinoline hat with sky blue ribbon bears an enormous sheaf of black and white roses, on which are fluttering bright. hued gaily-clad insects. Another rustic effect is seen in a tuft of reeds ornamenting a bronze straw; the dead reeds and green reeds surmounted by a large bird. Reeds woven into a crown, in peasant fashion, support the hat on the head and lessen the weight. A large toque of lavender blue tulle, crowned with westeria, is also knotted with reeds, and a number of straw hats in cream, bronze, maize' or pale blue are tied with blue ribbon and adorned with clusters of daisies round the crown and under the brim as a cachelleigne. Still, feathers have not been altogether discarded. Hats with horticultural exhibits, however, do not suit every face. Therefore, it is well for these that fickle fashion has not yet decreed the abolition of the feathers. I have seen one hat with several large feathers on the left side which I liked im- mensely. On the opposite side were similar bows of bright blue ribbon. The hat was of rough straw.

Coming down to the fashion for children, I may remark with regard to the hats that the sailor one still holds the palm. This fashion seems to vary less than any. The parents seem at last to have hit upon the right head-gear for their girls. The other day I saw one child in a dress which was of white flannel. It washes well and gets up each time like a new dress, so that it is particularly suitable for the present hot weather. They are really cut as a little coat and an ordinary plain skirt. Spotted white piqué costumes, with either blue or red pin spots, are made in a similar style, and they have in addition detachable collars, braided to match. These are attached with buttons, and can be taken off to be washed, and the coat itself is complete without the collar.

When you are thinking of washing curtains take note of the following hints :—First shake the our. talus until no more loose dust will shake off, then put them into a good, warm soap-suds and let them remain 24 hours. Now pour off the suds and put them into fresh, clean suds, each time squeezing the lace in parts when dipping it over and over again. Do not rub the lace on a board nor pound lb violently in the tub, but keep on renewing the suds and squeezing the fabric until clean. Now rinse in two clear waters, and finally id starch-water made by adding one gallon of moderately thick starch to one gallon of clear or blue water. This process of starching gives a more even result than the ordinary method. Stiffly-starched curtains are never used now.

div.head: " WOMEN'S CHAT."
div.p: " WOMEN'S CHAT."

The Queen who seems to have benefited greatly from her stay in the Highlands, will remain at Windsor for about three weeks, when she will proceed to Osborne. There, Her Majeety will receive visits from the various members of her family, the Duke and Duchess of Con- naught,and the Duke and Duchess of York being among her guests. When at Balmoral, the Queen's life is of the quietest, and this state of affairs seems—nowadays—to be more beneficial to Her Majesty's health than excitement in any shape or form. The Queen's messenger from Lon- don reaches the Castle each morning at half past six, but the contents of his despatch box are seldom brought to the notice of the Sovereign before ten o'clock, when she leaves the breakfast table. The next two or three hours are given unto business, then comes an airing in the grounds, the Queen in her donkey chair, and at two luncheon. At four the Queen leaves the Castle for her lengthy drive, after which an hour or so is devoted to reeding, working, or music. Dinner is served at nine, and rarely exceeds three quarters of an hour. The Queen's habit of driving at almost full speed makes it next to impossible for the aspiring photo- grapher to take successful snap-shots of Her Majesty, but it seems an amateur has! been fortunate enough to get a very excellent "shot "during the Sovereign's stay on Deeside. tie arranged his camera on a thick branch that commanded a good view of a road along which the Queen drives frequently. That afternoon the Royal carriage not only passed, but was stopped within a few yards of the tree to enable Her Majesty to draw the attention of her granddaughter, the Grand Duchess of Hesse to the beautiful view which may be had from that particular spot. This gave the young nhotograpaer the opportunity longed for, and ho secured three excellent negatives. There will be the customary gathering of members of the Danish Royal Family this coming autumn, but not at B.rnstorff. The loss of the Queen is all too keen and fresh for a meeting Chore to be possible to the King and his children, and so the reunion is to take place at Frsdenaborg which has been closed since the autumn of 1893 Fredensborg is an immense house on ttie Heroin- Leke, about seighteen miles from Copenbageneeand the autumn gatherings invariably took place here before the death of the late Emperor of Russia. Afterwards it was deemed desirable to hold them at Bernsterff, the latter house being lees full of painful memories to the Empress Dowager. The health of the Duke of Teck still remains most un- satisfactory and it is feared he will never now recover from the shock of his wife's death- To the Duchess of Yorkla telegram is despatched daily,and both Her Royal Highness and her brothers constantly visit their father. But he rarely even recognises them, and takes not the faintest interest in anything that goes on around him. His daily airings he takes in a bath chair, and never now emerges from the grounds of White Lodge. The artistic treasures stored away in White Lodge are considerable. Among the portraits is one of the late Duchess of Teek as a little girl, and another repre- sents the Duke of Cambridge as a chubby boy in High- land drees waving aloft the Union Jack. In the room that was the Duchess's boudoir, there is the portrait of the Duchess of York, peinted by the late Edwin Long, R.A., as well as a collection of miniatures that with the present fashion for these dainty keepsakes, would prob- ably command fabulous prices. The enamels are extra- ordinarily fine, and among them are some remarkable specimens after Holbein. Wonderful buhl furniture abounds, and of Sevres porcelain there are also many pieces of quite exceptional value and beauty, as well as some fine specimens of the Dresden art. Viennese paintings on mother o' pearl, pieces o; Black Forest pottery, Indian curiosities old and new, carved figures from the Tyrol, and Egyptian metal and woodwork, go to make up a collection it would be very difficult to equal. The number of Royal women devotsd to white toilettes is remarkable. The Queen of Italy rarely appears in a coloured gown,white being almost invariably worn by her Majesty, and the Princess of Naples has lately taken to following her Royal mother-in-law's example. The young Empress of Russia's preference for white is so great that she has come to be known as the "white Czarina," and the Queen of Roumania's taste in this direction is very similar. The Ddcliess of Fife prefers a white gown to any other, and Princess Henry of Battenburg holds the same opinion on this point. Up-to-date sleeves are still built skin tight, and with- out one atom of fullness on the top. The mode is far from a bee's/ming one to the majority of wonsen,to whom a little width on the shoulders is a great improvement. Moreover very tight sleeves cause the arms and hands to become red and puffy-locking, a scarcely desirable state of affairs. The best and wisest plan is—moderation. The very tight skirts are most unbocoming, as are also the very tight sleeves and capes. We should do well to follow the Princess of Wales' excellent example, and avoid all extremes in fashion which are usually neither becoming, nor in the test of taste. Washing silks are now everywhere obtainable at a price which makes them the competitors of cotton. The choice of colour too is wide, and altogether it would seem well to avail ourselves of so good an opportunity. There are often occasions when one hesitates to crush one's most treasured muslin blouse under a coat, for some part of the day, and yet wishes to enierge in greater radiance than en ordinary cotton blouse affords. There are moments when the washing silk blouse is a good friend. Pale Pink gauze veils are well to the fora again among cyclists. Some dotted all over with black, some with I white. They are exceedingly tiering to the sight, but this little (?) item does not seem to weigh one jot against their popularity. If a veil is worn at all, it should most emphatically be a plain, clear one, without dots of any kind, sort or description. Anything that dazzles the sight in the faintest degree is injurious, and should be avoided, as the p'ague. Some of the smartest pairs in equipages„this season,

Ido not match in colour. It is quite usual to see a mag- nificent pair in a park or mail phteton, one bay and one grey, one chestnut and one black-brown, one black and one white, This is distinctly a move in the right direc- tion. A perfectly matched pair, when they are obtain- able look splendid. When they are not, it seems more sensible to match them in quality and courage, than merely in coleu r. With regard to Ole bearing rein, this seems to he loss in evidenee, and the improvement has prabably been brought about by the Duke of Portland, who has once more protested against the practice of tor- turing horses in this manner. Mountaineering is, at the present time recommended by many of our leading doctors, for girls with delicate chests, and several instances are recorded of a complete recovery, when all other "cures" had failed. Be this as it may, mountaineering is a very fascinating exercise, and with proper precautions and tried skill, there is no reason why it should be any mere risky than many other kinds of sport in whieh the element of danger necessarily enters. Among the Alpine heights there is now a regular epidemic of tunnels and railways, and very shortly it will no doubt be possible to take a ticket at any of our great railway stations, that will see us safely tl the top of any peak in Switzeiland. RED CURRANT CHARLOTTE.—Butter a pie dish, cover the bottom and sides of it with thin slices of buttered bread, place some red currants on the bread with some sugar. Proceed with these layers until the dish is full, bake in a quick oven until the currants are quite tender. Tura on to a dish, sift some sugar over, and serve.

div.head: LONDON IN MONTE CARLO.
div.p: LONDON IN MONTE CARLO.

English visitors to Monte Carlo will be glad to find that Messrs. Benoist and Foucault, of the Princes' Res- taurant, Piccadilly, have provided for their comfort at this fashionable Mediterranean resort. The Restaurant which they and their friends have opened has already been patronised by members cf many European Royal families, and by the most distinguished men and women of all countries who have lately been sojourning there, including the Prince ot Wales and the Duke of Cam- bridge. Taken as a business enterprise, it may be re- garded favourably, because th Piccadilly concern,under the same management, has been steadily paying 10 per cent. ever since it commenced. What will interest the great majority of travellers is the fact that a centre of refined comfort, such as they have learnt to appreciate in Piccadilly, has been established in Monte Carlo. The Company now forming to exploit this intends to increase and improve its accommodation by building a new hotel capable of receiving four hundred guests. "The Her- mitage Hotel and Restaurant," is the title adopted.— The Observer.

div.head: SEAFARERS:
div.p: THE SEAFARERS:
A MODERN ROMANCE.

BY JOHN BLOUNDELLE-BURTON, Author of "Fortune's rny Foe," "The Scourge of God," "Across the Salt Seas," "The Clash of Arms," "In the Day of Adversity," "A Gen- tleman Adventurer," "His Own Enemy,* "Denounced," &c.
CHAPTER XXI.
WAS lIED ASHORE.

They had both slept again by the time that the morning broke with the suddenness of the tropics, and with the, coming of the sun, heralded by the pale primrose-green hue that all who have been twixt Capricorn and Cancer know so well, this followed by the vermilion and golden shafts of light, and then the deep blood-rod tinge suffusing all the horizon. They had slept uneasily, each in their place; with, outside, near the opening tu the little cave under the knoll, the tiger lying tranquilly as though keeping watch and ward over her whom, probably, it deemed its friend and mistress. Yet, ever and again, as she, awakening to regard it more than once—because of the fear which Stephen's words had engendered in her mind—saw very well, with the yellow eyes peering out restlessly from their closed slits of eyelids, the iris of each eye itself a vertical slit also. And she acknowledged that Charke had spoken aright, that the time had come for the creature to be either imprisoned or made away with. All its evil instincts were undoubtedly being developed with its growth; soon they would have obtained their full force and be, perhaps, exerted. It was time.

But now the dawn was come, the blood-red of the Eastern sky was plainly visible, and the birds of the island were twittering to each other and pluming themselves ; whereon the girl rose and left the cave, passing by the creature lying so close to her as though in fear of arousing it. In actual fear of it, indeed, not knowing but that it might turn and rend her at any momnt. For it was big enough and strong enough to dcr so now, its size being that of a large retriever, or a year old mastiff; she, or he, even—that stalwart muscular sailor—would probably have had little chance against it if it had set upon them. Both were unarmed, and both were tweakened and broken down by their struggles in the tempest-tossed waves.

Charke, seeing the girl rise from her recumbent position, rose also, quickly and quietly, and came towards her, while as he did so he said: "Now, to-day is the time for me to make that search round the island which I promised you. We will but eat a little fruit, aml then I will set out."

"Shall I go with you ? " she asked, as, taking up the cocoanut shell she turned to go towards the rivulet that ran at her feet, "or is it better for me to remain here? Perhaps, too, it may be more than I can do. Or, indeed," she hastened to add, "more than you can accomplish in one day, and in such heat as there will be. Oh, Mr. Charke," she continued, "you are not strong enough to undertake it yet!" "I feel strong enough this morning," he replied, "and, if I cannot make the whole tour of the place in one day, I can at least do a considerable part of it. I will begin at once, before the sun becomes too fierce. But, as for you, perhaps it would be best if you stayed here. The outlook from this portion of the island is,l think, the one from which any ship that happened to pass would be most likely to be observed. You see, we look west from here, towards where Africa lies, and vessels use that track in preference to running more out into the open." "I will do anything you suggest," she said. "Anything you think will be for the best. Only" —and again there came upon her face that stricken look which made his heart so sad for her, and which, whenever he observed it, caused him to bury every sorrow of his own in a more profound and unselfish one for her—" only—you know—l—l—at present—just at present—for a day or so—do not wish to see a ship come here to rescue us." "I know, I know," he answered, not daring to keep his eyes fixed full upon that lovely, but unhappy face. "I know. Well, we will not look out for rescue yet. But, still, I think you had better stay here. We do not know for certain the size of this island; it is only guess work on my part. It may be too far a walk, too much of an undertaking for you. "You are not afraid—of that? " he continued, as he directed his eyes towards Bengalee, seeing how, while he was speak- ing, she, too, had let her glance fall upon the cub, which was now pacing restlessly about at their feet. _

"No," she said, "I am not. Yet what you said in the night was true. It is growing beyond con- trol, and, of course, I know how treacherous and savage these animals are. It was a piece of girlish folly on my part to beg poor uncle to save it." "I scarcely know how we are to make away with it," he replied. "I have nothing but this "—and he took from his pocket a little white-handled penknife, which he had probably bought for a shilling off a card when exposed in a London shop- window. "I could hardly kill it with that. How- ever, one thing is certain, it will die of starvation ere long on this island It cannot live on fruit as we can, nor catch birds, and there are no signs of animals, not even rats or mice, as far as I can see." _

"Oh, poor thing ; what a dreadful death to die!" the girl exclaimed, her pity awakened for a creature which had been more or less her pet for some few weeks. Yet she hastened to ask if starvation did not make such animals even more fierce than usual, and if the risk to them both would not, thereby, be increased. Then, before he could reply, she suddenly exclaimed, as her glance fell on the sea: "What is that out there? Surely—surely—it is not a drowned man? Oh! not that. Not that!" Following the direction of that glance, he saw something drifting about on the tranquil, almost rippleless, water over which by now the rays of the risen sun were gleaming horizontally. Something that, since it was end on towards them and the island, was not easily to be distinguished yet, was all the same, undoubtedly no drowned man nor human body, alive or dead. At first he thought it might be a dead shark—his knowledge of the sea telling him at once that it was not a living one, since they never expose aught but the dorsal fin when swimming—then, a second later, he recog- nised what the object was. "No," he exclaimed, anxious to appease her terrors at once—knowing also to whom, above all others, to whose dead body those terrors pointed, "No, that is no body, living or dead. Instead, it is one of our qwarter-boats. Washed out of the chocks when the ship turned on her side, no doubt, and floating about ever since." "It is coming nearer," Bella exclaimed, her eyes still on it and full of delight, at hearing that in it there was, at least, no confirmation of one awful fear; "do you not think so ? " "Undoubtedly it is coming nearer. It will strike the shore just there if the reef does not catch it " ; and he pointed with sailor-like certainty to a spot close by. "It will be a mercy if it does." "Why? We could not escape :from this place in that, could we ? " "Hundreds of sailors have escaped death in smaller boats than that; aye! and lived for many days, too, on an open and rough sea in such. But it is not for that only. If it comes ashore I can make a visit to the poor old Emperor and find out something, if not all, that I—that we—want to know. Also, though we need not put to sea in it, we may use it to get to some other island which is inhabited, by, perhaps, white men; but, any- how, by someone. It will be of the greatest assistance, especially as, since it floats, it must be undamaged. I trust the oars, if not the sail, are in it." And now, listening to his words, Bella became as eager for the quarter-boat to come ashore as her companion was and, together, they went down to the spot he had indicated as that which the boat was likely to arrive at—a spot about sixty yards from where they were. As Bella walked by her preserver's side she was wondering many things, wondering if he would, indeed, be able now to discover what the fate of the others in the Emperor had ; been, and, above all, if, by the aid of this i boat, he would be enabled to solve for her the ques- tion she hourly, momentarily, asked herself by day and night—the question whether there was any hope left of a life of happiness and bliss to be passed by her lover's side, or whether, for her, the future could bring nothing now but a joyless, heart- broken existence. Also, she mused upon one other thing, namely, what he was thinking of while, with his eyes never off the incoming boat, he meditated deeply as, from his knit brows and fixed look, she felt sure he was doing. The thoughts, those that actually were in his mind, he would, undoubtedly, not have divulged. even though she had asked hi=

to ao so, since they here such es could only nave caused her grief unspeakable. For he was thinking bat, since this quarter-boat had been washed °al of the chocks and off the deck into the sea, ana had then floated about for forty-eight hours in the neighbourhood previous to being directed by some subtle current to the island, so other things that were on that 'deck would be subject to the F ame conditions. The bodies of drowned men ;the body of her lover! Ho knew that the sea and its currents and tides work in calm weather with as much regularity as the sun and the moon work in their rising, and their setting, even, indeed, as the seasons themselves work; and he knew, also, that if Gilbert's body—which was close to where the quarter-boat rested when the ship struck—had been washed into the sea at the same time as it, then it was most probable, nay, almost certain, that it also would come ashore at the same spot and per- hails almost at the same time. What horror, what a fresh horror, would that be for this poor devoted girl to experience! For, in his own heart, he never doubted for one moment that somewhere close at hand the body of Gilbert Bampfyld was floating about. The boat was coming very close into the shore row, so close that they could see that one oar was in it, but no more; also, that there was nothing else, as well as that the rudder was not fixed in the braces. Yet that mattered little to Stephen Charke if he could only once get possession of the boat itself, since, with one oar on such a glassy sheet of water as this ocean was now he could easily enough propel and steer it. "I am glad, thankful, it is coming ashore," he said now. "I had thought of swimming out to the ship only I dreaded the sharks. Little use as one's life may be, one would scarcely care to lose it by the jaws of those brutes." And, though he did not see it, the girl by his side gave him a glance such as would, perhaps, have cheered his heart had he done so. Was not her own life, also, of little enough use, she asked herself as he spoke, to make her sympathise with his remark? Would it not be a broken and dejected one, henceforth, if that which she dreaded, which she had almost forced herself to feel sure must be the case, should be proved beyond all doubt before many more hours had passed? For every hope with which she had buoyed herself up was sinking tn her breast, as moment after moment went by, and the time grew longer and longer since the wreck had taken place. The boat touched the white, pebbly beach now, grating on it with a gentle scrape, and Stephen, who had gone close to the water's edge to await its arrival, put out his hand and, seizing first the stem and then the painter, drew it a foot or two further on shore. Then he got into it, and, grasp- ing the solitary oar which had remained in the boat simply because the loom, or handle, had got caught beneath the stern thwart, prepared to shove off in it. _ _ _

"You will not mind," he said, as he did so, "being left alone for half an hour? This will not take me away from you for so long as when I go round the island." While she, in answer shook her head to indicate that she was not at all afraid of being ',aft by herself.
CHAPTER XXII. A sArLos's /MIT.

"She is perfectly` sound and watertight," 4e called back to her as, with the hand which was uninjured, he threw the oar over the boat's stern, and worked her out from the shore. "If we want her to help us off to another island, she will do it, if I can only find another oar floating about some- where."

Then he propelled her as swiftly as he could to where the Emperor of the Moon lay outside the rock, her keel and copper bottom gleaming in the bright morning sun. As he drew near to the ship:he began to perceive how all hope mnst be abandoned of the likelihood that anyone should still be alive and imprisoned in the ship. She had turned over even more than he had at first imagined after regarding her from the shore of the island, so that almost was that keel level in a manner exactly the opposite from what sailors mean when they talk about a "level keel." It stuck up now, as far as it was out of water, like some sharp mountain ridge when re- garded by those who are in a valley beneath; form- ing an almost horizontal line while, beneath the keel and above the water, for half the length of the vessel, was visible a portion of the outside of the main hold, down to (or up from) her diagonal ribboned-lines. And here was a great gaping wound, a hole smashed into her side large enough to have let the whole Indian Ocean pour into the devoted ship directly it was made, and, although there might well be others which were not visible, sufficient to have filled and sunk forthwith the greatest vessel that was ever launched. The force of the impact was to be appreciated, too, by the manner in which her copper sheathing was forced into her and burst, so that, where the blow had been struck by the jagged tooth of the rock, the latter looked like a destroyed ehevaux de frise, or, for a better com- parison, a paper hoop through which an acrobat had passed. And, in this burst and broken protec- tion, as in other and less terrible circumstances, it might have been (though naturally it had proved useless here) the sheathing nails stuck out like brilliant, gleaming yellow teeth, all broken and distorted. - -

Charke brought the quarter-boat alongside the upturned, or leaning, bottom, so that, by looking through this gaping wound, he could peer into the now reversed decks and see that, on what had once been the roof of it, but was now the floor, a moss of articles, such as is usually stowed away in a ship's lower depths, lay. A mass, composed of cables and old and new sails, also some stores, con- sisting of dozens of tinned-meat cans unopened, boxes of sardines, and so forth, and several old sea chests and trunks all lying, of course, helter skelter, as they had been thrown together by the ship's reversal. "There are some things of use here," Charke thought, "and worth taking away," whereupon he ran the painter through a small hole in the sheathing and tied it tightly, and then scrambled up the vessel's inverted . side until he was able to drop himself through the opening into the deck, taking care that he tore neither his flesh nor his clothes in doing so. Being there, he selected a small sail which he found; it was, indeed, a boat sail, and having its gear of mast and tackle attached, while passing it through the orifice, he dropped it carefully into the boat, and next he took a few of the tins of provisions, and dropped them into her, too. And also he found something which would be to him, in the utterly unprovided condition in which Bella and he had escaped to the island, of the greatest service. This was a long, sharp knife, in its leather sheath, such as sailors strap to their sides, and new and in good condition, so that he did not doubt that the last seaman who had been sent below to this deck had dropped it there, and he was able to picture to himself the man's annoyance, probably expressed aloud and with a good deal of vehemence and strong language, over his loss. This done—and the doing of it had not taken long—he prepared to leave the disordered bold, when he remembered that there was one thing he wanted, namely, some cable. "That tiger has to die at on," lie muttered to himself. "With piece of stout rope and this knife—which would slay anything, from an elephant downwards—it's death should not be difficult of accomplishment." Then, having selected two or three pieces of cable of different strands, he got out through the hole again and into the boat. It is almost needless to write down that he found no sign of human life as he rowed about and round the wrecked Emperor of the Moon for some moments afterwards. Needless, too, perhaps, to add that he had never expected to find any. He was a sailor, accustomed to disaster at sea and full also of much acquired knowledge pertaining to many of the calamities which it had never been his lot to experience heretofore ; and he knew—felt sure, and would have staked his life upon the certainty of his convictions—that of all who had been in that doomed ship an hour before she struck, none except Bella Waldron and himself were now alive. Those who had beee below in the cabins or saloon, those also who were in forecastle or galley had met, must have met, not only with their deaths but their graves at one and the same time; while as for the unhappy and blind young officer who had caused him so much heartache by winning the woman whom he loved so fondly and whom he hsd once hoped to win—why! it was impossible that he should still be alive. If he had been washed ashore, it could be only as a corpse, and it was most im- probable that even that should have happened. In truth, he believed that, with all the others, he had been carried below by the overturning of the ship and then pinned down, buried beneath the mass of the fabric. Otherwise, since the boat had floated ashore, so, too, would he have done by now. "The woman he had hoped to win," he repeated softly to himself, as still he sculled the quarter boat round and round, 'peering down into the dark blue depths as far as he could penetrate; endeavour- ing also to perceive some sign or memorial—even so much as a cap or straw hat—of one of those 'nor drowned sailors imprisoned below "the

woman he had hoped to win ! " And, as tne phrase rose to his mind, though not to his lips, he recalled also how he had cherished the thought of the length of voyage that had lain before her ere she could ioin her lover in India • how, too, he had. pondered .on half a hundred things which mignv happen ere the old Emperor should be anchored in Bombay Harbour. Almost, now, those medi- tations seemed to have been prophetic—for what had not happened! The girl's lover was gone, removed by death, and she had none other in the world on whom to lean but himself. And what was more, she spoke kindly to him; pitied him, he could well perceive; there was something between them now, a deep sympathy, a reliance on each other in their misfortunes, which had never existed before. "The woman he had hoped to win!" Well!—he scarce dared whisper the thought to his longing heart, yet it was there !—the thought, the hope that in days to come, in after months, perhaps years, when her grief for Gilbert Bampfyld was mellowed and softened by time, when she knew him better, and should fully recognise how profound his adoration for her was, he might still win her! She could not, young as she was, and with all the years of a long life before her, sorrow for ever— sorrow for a memory that would at last be nothing but a shadow. _ _

"He would win her!" he said aloud to himself now, as he worked the boat ashore, "he was resolved he would." The one obstacle in his path was removed, the brave, gallant young officer was gone, brushed aside by Fate. He would win her yet t He stepped ashore now to where she was standing watching him, and almost, it seemed—if his recent thoughts had not tinged with a roseate hue his present fancies—that there was a look of greeting and of welcome in her eyes to him, even, as she saw that he had come back—at the ending of so short an absence as his had been. Was she beginning even now, now that she had none other in the world to watch for—to desire to have him always near her. Ahl if that were indeed so! Then —then he might win her at last. "You found," she asked, speaking low, and in those sad tones which had come into her voice of late, and since disaster had fallen heavily on them, "you found no sign of any others having been saved ? "

"No," he said, also softly. "No, there are no signs of that. Miss Waldron—l am neither cruel nor hard of heart, but, oh! how can I say itt—it is useless to hope." "Useless! Ah, well, I suppose it is—must be And, God help me, must also be borne," then she turned away from him with the desire to hide the tears which had risen to her eyes from' being seen by him, and went back to the shade of the trees under which she had been sitting until she saw the quarter-boat returning with him in it. And he followed her, carrying the cable which he brought away from the ship; the knife which he had found being in his pocket, and the sail with its gear left in the boat. The sun was terribly fierce now, so fierce that to be beneath its rays for only a few moments was to risk sunstroke and to be burnt red, as he had long since been, and she, since her exposure on the island; and, of course, he could not attempt the projected tour of the place until it once more sank low in the west. There was, there— fore, nothing now to do but to sit idly gazing out to sea, watching for signs of any ship which might pass near enough to see them when they should have erected signals. "After the tour round theiisland," he said to her, as he sat by her side beneath the palm trees and occupied his time in plaiting some of the long, thick grass which grew at their feet into something that should serve for hats, or, at least, coverings for their heads, "after the tour, when we have had the last sad satisfaction of knowing that there can be none who have escaped, you will not object to my endeavouring to arrange for our being taken off? The Mozambique Channel is full of shipping on its way to India during the time of the south-west monsoon—you will let me make signals, will you not? "

"I am in your hands," she replied, her eyes on him. "You must do all that you think best. Ali! Mr. Charke, you do not know how grateful I feel to you." "Never say that. Not a word. I knew, I thought, I could save one besides myself, and, naturally," he went on simply, "I saved you." Then both sat on musing and meditating in silencr; "Here comes the tiger," he said now, seeing the creature stalking towards them in the lithe, treacherous manner peculiar to its race. "I imagine it has been endeavourift to find food. I brought off some tinned things from the ship yet, cruel as it seems to be, it is not advisable, I think, to give it anything in the shape of flesh. Mean- while, if it will only go to sleep we ought to secure it," and as he spoke he took up one of the pieces of cable and commenced tying what is known to sailors as a double-diamond knot. But, previously, he had fastened the other end securely round one of the palm trees that grew close by him. "There will be one advantage in this," he said, "namely, that the more it pulls against it the tighter will come the loop, so that its intelligence will prevent it from straining at the rope and strangling itself." "Poor wretch," Bella exclaimed, "how gaunt and lean it is growing! I recognise that it cannot be kept alive or even taken off with us when we are found here; yet—yet I am sorry for it." "Yes," he answered, "I understand that, but it has to be done—must be done—is imperative. In the state it is now in from hunger, and also owing to its increasing strength, our lives are no longer safe with it, and certainly not with it at large; while, if one of us were to scratch our hands, or oven get the slightest wound, and the creature smelt the blood, which it would undoubtedly do—well I the result might be terrible. Now, see, it is going to sleep, appears exhausted. I must drop the loop over its head." "No," she answered, "let me do that. It is still very docile with me," and, as she spoke, she took the loop from his hand,while, patting the creature's head—whereon it raised it as a dog will raise its head when stroked by a loved hand—she dropped it down until the rope was round its neck, though not without muttering some words of regret as to what she deemed her treachery. "It is no treachery," he said, "no more treachery, indeed, than to tie up a mastiff in its kennel. And, even though it were, it would not matter. These creatures are themselves the incarnation of treachery. However, the main point is that it is now secure. It is not yet strong -enough to burst this rope." Such was the case, yet it was strange that to so acute a mind as Charke's there had not occurred the idea that it would not take a tiger very long to gnaw a ship's rope through, if it desired it* release.

div.head: NEWS OF THE GAME.
div.p: NEWS OF THE GAME.

We understand that H. Freedman, the Scottish Champion, proposes to go to New York on comple- tion of his present tour in England. Mr. Seigel, of Brazil, Ind., is at prasent en a visit to England. The following extract from the 4. Dis- patch " may, therefore, prove of service to the ' members of some of our draughts clubs : SAM SEIGEL, BRAZIL, ISO. Oile day last weak a mild-mannered, pleasant- spoken, -elderly gentleman called at the Home Hotel, Pittsburg, and ing,nred for J.P. Reed. Karr, (the hotel's big, good-natured boy) replied " Reed is not around just now, btu he'll be here after a while. In the meantime, if you play checkers, I'll try to amuse you." The stranger smiled and sat down, and, Bail Ktrr, when telling the tale later on, "I thought I had a soft mark, as he about mid-game threw ma a man fur no apparent reason. At the finish I was still a man to the good, but the stranger won the game. The next game also broughta me an early gift. but I thought 'Old fellow, you're n Indian giver ;" and threw it back ;shortly after he had tried the same trick, but I would not stand it, and once more gave back the man, and for the third time he pressed the gift ou my reluctant acceptance. I was afraid of it, and seeking a plan to return but could see no safe way of doing so, when Reed came in and remarked: "Its lucky you have the extra man, Karr, or you'd lose." The stranger remarked if I can force an exchange, I'll win." The exchange was not in evielence and a draw was allowed me. I shook myself and told Reed to take my place. Reed did so, and after a very pretty game, lasting about an hour, the stranger woo. He then remarked : "I'm very berry but my train for Buffalo,N.Y., is about due, and I cannot stay any longer." "Who am I?" (to Karr), "I leave you my card as a reminder of my first visit to the Home Hotel.'" The card r3sd as in the a bove caption.

The small diagram will enable our resders to understand the notation by which the sauces of the game are recor:led. Black no uples the squares num- bered 1 to 12 and white those numbered 21 to 32. The figures thus (11-15) indicate that a move is made from and to the squares to nnmbered.Black has the opening move and the pairs of figures apply alternately to Black and White to the close.

WARRINGTON CORPORA- TION BILL IN PARLIAMENT. CON CLUSION OF COMUITTEE PROCEEDINGS.
THE BILL PASSED.

When the Police and Sanitary Committee oa Tuesday resumed the consideration of this Bill, Sir Stafford Northcote in the chair, it was with the full exp?ctation that the seventh day's examination of the measure would complete their work.

PURCHASE OF ADDITIONAL LANDS.-.VICTORIA PARR. The promoters brought up a new clause giving the Cor- poration power to purChase additiJnal lands by agree- ment as follows :—"Tne Corporation may purchase by agreement, in addition to the lands which they are by this Act authorized to take by compulsion, any lands not exceeding in the whole 100 acres, that is to say—for waterworks purposes, 40 acres ; for the purpose of the street widenings and improvements and the widening and extension of footways or highways authorized by this Act, one acre ; for the purpose of a site for new police court buildings and stations and of the necessary buildings thereon, two acres; for the purpose of a public park and open spaces, 53 acres; for the purpose of and in connection with the extension of the hospital for in- fectious diseases belonging to the Corporation, two acres ; for the purpose of river wharves, one acre ' • for the purpose of a site for a technical institute and the buildings necessary for technical instruction and second- ary education, •ne acre. Provided that the Corperation shall not create or permit the creation of a nuisance on any such lands,and such lands shall not be used for any building except it is required for or used in connection with the undertakings of the Corporation. Mr. BovcE(for the Local Government Board) urged the Committee that in regard to the Park, the land to be acquired or that had been acquired should be specifically mentioned in the Bin.
_ Mr. Stephens, Q.C., for the promoters. sg.id that thl Bill by vacious clauses clearly showed that Victoria Park was intended. _ _ _ _
• Mr. LEurY (ona of the Committee) said that in one clause tiae new park wts spoken of as " to W.+ called Victoria Park." Should no: the promoters strike out the " to be?''

Mr. STEPHENS agreed to strike out these two words. Mr. BOYCE then urged ttiat it was against precedent for the Committee to leave in such vague general powers as to allow the Corporation to acquire by agreement one acre for the purpose of street widening's, & ~ authorised by the Bill. All these street widenings were under com- pulsory powers. Mr. STEPHENS submitted that this power was advisa- b!ei so that a street improvement could not be spoiled for want of any power to acquire land by agreement. Mr. Bows: : A clause unless it defines toe p irticular sites:with which it intends to deal is absolutely without p recedent. Mr. STEPHENS said he could quote 20 Water Acts in which there were general powers to acqairei by agree- ment in addition to the cornpuis )ry powers. If the Committee felt strongly about it ne would not persi et, but he would sabrnit it was not an unreasonable pro- posal. Mr. H. J. WILSON (one of the Committee) remarked that if it was without precedent for the Coalnattee to grant a general power of this sort, it did not matter whether it applied to one or to ten acres. Mr. LONGDIN, borough surveyor, produced, at the re- quest of the Ctiairman,the plan of the proposed improve- ments. _ ,

Mr. STEPHENS said that in the Blackburn Act of fast Year thero were precisely the same powers to take land by agreement. Mr BOYCE : They did pot take borrowing power for such land as Warrington now proposed. Mr. STEPHENS contended that Blackburn had practic- ally borrowing power for such purposes. Mr. MliEux.s. (a member of the Committee) said that the power to take by agreement was for improvements "authorised by this Act." They had vimpulsory powers for everything authorizA within the lines of deviation ;f and this further power to take by agre:,rnent could not authorize them to do anything outside the lines o deviation. _ _ .

The Committee struck out the words "for the purpose of the street widenings and improvements and the widening and extension of footways auttior.zed by this act, one acre," and with regard to the public park they altered it to "&r the purpose of Victoria park, 53 acres." The reference to the land for the hospital ex- tension was struck out, this matter being dealt with under another clause, and on the Chairman remarking that evidence was given that the agreement with regard to river wharves was only for a querter of an acre, that liiit ef laud was put in the new clause instead of one acre.

Mr. PEMBROKE STEPHENS HOW brought this clause again before the Committee, and said that opinions seemed to be somewhat divided upon this que3tion and that it had been suggested to the Corporation that they perhaps had not given proper weight to the statements in the report of the Home Office urging that the matt?r should be dealt with by a public, and not by a local Bill. The Committee had been pleased to entertain the clause, but looking at the rrittcr all round, the Corpora- tion had come to the bona-fide conclusion that it would be inexpedient to press the clause at present. They did not abandon its principle, and looked to public legisla- tion which would give effect to it, but in the actusl cir- cumstances they asked the Committee to strike out the clause, the Corporation, of course, retaining the right should public legislation not be passed to come subse- quently with a renewal of the proposal; The clause was thereupon struck out of the Bill.

div.head: REPAYMENT OF MONET.
div.p: REPAYMENT OF MONET.

Mr. JOHN FAIRHURST, borough treasurer, re-called, stated that the terms for the repayment of the money borrowed for the purposes of the Act were those ordin- arily sanctioned by Parliament. Fifty years were taken for the repayment of the loans in connection with the police courts, hospital, sanitary depot, and street im- provements. and 60 years for the waterworks and park. The committee were now asked to give five years' in- terval before payments into the sinking fund for the waterworks expenditure should commence, but the wit- ness said that if they found they could begin the re- payments earlier they would do so, as they had done so with regard to previous sinking funds. It all depended upon whether the new works began to be remunerative. The CHA.IRMAN asked why the original Bill contained no such proposal. Mr. PgranizoKE STEPHENS said that through some over- sight the original clause did not contain the provision, and that on the promoters suggesting a suspension for ten years, Lord Morley, chairman of the Committees of the House of Lords,s3id he could not consent to a period of more than five years. Mr. BOYCE said it was most unusoal for the Committes to give a suspension of the commeacement of the sink- ing fund. Mr. H. J. WILSON (one of the Committee) remarked that now the heavy expenditure of the Daresbury work had been struck out there did not seem to he any necess- ity for any suspension of the sinking fund. The, Committee refused to allow any period of suspen- sion of the sinking fund.

After Mr. E. MANSERGII had he-n heard on ths nature of the oxnenditure on the water works,and h had stated that £30,000 would be spent on the pumping stations at Winwick for the domestic supply The Committee reluced the period of repayment for the waterworks expenditure from 60 to 50 years.
PE EP NITUIL ANNUITIES.

On the clause for the conversion of existing, perpetual annuities, Councillor SHAW GREEN. Chairman of the Finance Committee of the Corporation, was called, and explained that these annuities were part of the purchase money of the as works, purchased under the Act of 1877. By that Act the Corporation could purchase the annuities at the maximum price of 25 years, but while many holders sold, others did not, and still refwei to sell, although under the local Act of 1890 the market price was substi- tuted for the 25-years period. Tee Corporation now pro- posed that at the end of 25 years' time, they could call upon the hvldere to sell at the present market value of 33 1-3 years' purchase. They ,thought that only fair, as they were bound to provide a sinking fund to pay off the gasvrorks debt in 60 years. The Committee refused the clause. After going through the various clauses the Committee passed the Bill, and ordered it to be reported to the House as amended.

div.head: BLACK DOG.
div.p: THE BLACK DOG.

"Then the black deg got on to my Mack, and stuck there all day," said Robert Louis Stevenson. In plain English, be was in a fat of profound molan choly. There are no end of things that tend to make us low-spirited. We don't discuss them. You know what they look like as well as I do. When the black dog wants to climb on our backs, he uses some of these things as a staircase. I allude now to outside reasons and causes, such as loss of friends, of money, etc., etc. But we often feel the mercury going down in our mental barometer, with- out seeing or ezperiencing a cause for it. We some- times fancy it a warning of trouble ahead, and worry as if we had consciously walked over the spot where we are booked to be buried. We try to shake off the brood- ing impression, but it hangs on, like Mr. Stevenson's black dog. What is it that sends our spirits down into our boots and makes a familiar tread sound like the approach of an undertaker? Perhaps we can cull the idea out of the letters (both short) of two women. " For over twenty years," runslcne of them," I suffered from biliousness. A good deal of the time I felt heavy and tired, and CO low-spirited and sad that the earth seemed dressed in sackcloth. Everything bad the hue of evil, present or to come. After meals I had an awful pain at the chest and through to the shoulders I had fearful headtchea, and when the bilious attack. came on I was prostrate. " For hours together I would be deadly sick—retch- ing and straining; but all I brought up was a bitter, nasty fluid. About every fortnight I had these spells, and they made me very weak. No matter what diet I took I was just as bad. I liked liver pills and medicine of all kinds, but sawdust or water would have done me as much good. "At last a gentleman at Hertford told me of Mother Seigel's Syrup, ane said it was the only real and effective remedy for liver complaint he had ever seen or heard of. On the strength of what he said I got a bottle, and it made me better than I bad been for time out of mind. It cleared the bile out of my system and caused my liver to act naturally, and as it should. It lifted a load off me, and made me feel light, high-spirited, and happy. Since that time I have enjoyed good health. If liver trouble ever comes on me again—as I think and hope it will not—l shall take down my bottle of Mother Seigel's Syrup and seek no furtber. I know it will set matters right." (Signed) Mrs. ANNIE SEERING, Wertnley, near Broxbourae, Herta, February 3, 1899.

" In June, 1895," writes another frank and intelligent woman, " I seemed to have run into a region of dulness, weakness, and gloom. What ailed me I could not sur- mise. My skin began to turn yellow, and so did my eyes. I had no appetite, and was frequently sick with pain at the chest after eating. I craved food, yet the very sight of it repelled and disgusted me. "I lost sleep until I suffered from habitual insomnia, and my spirits sank until as if nc,thing hopeful or cheer- ful was left in the world. As for ever being well and strong again, I gave up expecting it. "In this way my life dragged along month after month. A relative of mine, Mrs. limes, of Bourne heath, then told me how she had been cured of a similar complaint by,Mother Seigel's Syrup, after having vainly tried everything else she could think of. So I com- menced using it, and found relief in so brief a time as to surprise me. _ _ . _

" This was evidently the true and right medicine for the stomach and liver. My bad symptoms and feelings grow less and less until I could eat and digest and not suffer. After having taken throe or four battles of the syrup I was in health once more, with my heart full of thankfulness and my mouth full of praise for the medi- cine that had done so much for me. You are free to make my letter public if you think best." (Signed) (Mrs.) ELIZLESZTEL FIRLD, Catsbill, near Bromegrove, Wiwi., July 21, 1898. Nine times out uf ten the Black Dog is a torpid liver. Drive him away with a few good doses of Mother Seigel's Syrup.

div.head: FARM FIRE AT PRESTON BROOK.
div.p: FARM FIRE AT PRESTON BROOK.

On Sunday afternoon information was received at the Warrington Fire Br,gade Station, that a fire had broken out on the farm of Mr. Robert it-lhep- herd, Parkside Farm, Aston, near Preston Brook. The deputy-superintendent (Mr. Frank Turner, jun.), and a good complemnt of men, with the en- gine " Major" at once proceeded to the farm, and found that a stack of straw was on fire in a Dutch barn. They directed their eiforts to prevent the flames spreading to several other stacks in close proximity ; and in this attempt they were succesb.- Jul. The stack of straw was, however, totally des- troyed. The damage is covered by IA surance. The fire is supposed to be the work of an incendiary.

BREAKFAST AND SUPPER.
AN OLD WARRINGTON INSTITUTION.
A. VISIT TO THE BLUE COAT SCHOOL.
[l3v " QUILP N.l

The Warrington Blue Coat Sc-nool occupies the whole side of a quiet street—named after the in- stitution—and immediately opposite St. Ann's Church, Winwick-road. This is not, in all proba- bility, information to ninety per cent of our readers, but it is, at any rate, a definite fact which no one can take exception to, and also serves the purpose of a formal introduction to this article. In these years when opportunities for education are unlimited, and the siOjects taught bewildering in their variety and number, the Warrington Blue Coat School serves as a strong and interesting link with the past. Should you at any time have cause to visit this Institution you will find there are two modes of entrance into the same. One, a gate- way, which is chiefly used by the trades- men during the week, and for visitors on Sunday, as it leads directly to the church. The latter statement requires a further explanation. It is customary for parents and friends to attend service in the church on Sunday evenings in com- pany with the little ones. As the day of my visit was not Sunday I paused at the other entrance which happens to be the first, and finding the door closed gave notice of my arrival by pressing a very insignificant-looking little button. In answer to my summons a little maiden, who in demeanour but not in appearance strongly reminded me of the " Marchioness," opened the door and with becoming dignity ushered me into the board room where the trustees hold their periodical meetings. The little maid disappeared and whilst I was examining some of the excellent oil paintings of benefactors of the Blue Coat School en the walls of the room, which was furnished in old oak with quaint high-backed chairs, Mr. Rosa arrived. The latter gentleman, who was kindness itself, immediately prepared to show me over the build- ing, and let me here say, those who rashly form I conclusions as to the size of the same from a sur- i vey outside, will findlthemselves mistaken on an inspection of the building inside. As a matter of fact, it appeared about three or four times the size I believed it to be from a survey at the front. Some little of the history of the Institution will probably not Come amiss at this point. The origin of the Warrington Bluecoat School was a very humble one. In the year 1665, Mr. John Allen, a native of Warrington, but then resident in St. Mar- garet's, Westminster, made known his intention of leaving a legacy for the purpose of apprenticing " fire several poore boys to some useful handi- craft trade." On the death of Mr. Allen in 1677, the legacy of £lBO was paid, and at a public meet- ing of the inhabitants convened about this time, it was decided to raise funds to be employed in the extension of the plan. The trustees thus applied them. Divested of the quaintness of the old Eng- lish language of that time the s,bjects were: To put poor children to apprenticeships; to send up students to the Universities ; to relieve poor old people ; to cure the lame and diseased; to pay rents for the poor ; to clothe poor children ; to prefer them to services; to carry poor children to Ireland; and to pay for the table of poor children. These were the noble objects for which this Institution was first formed, and it was in the sear 1711, that this charity was first constituted an educational one. In the year mentioned (1711), 24 boys were put to school and at the age of 14 were put to apprenticeship with new clothes, bible and common prayer book. The" Blew" boys, as they were then called attended as day scholars, the old Charity School (situated in the centre of the town behind Trinity IChurch), until the opening of the present building in 1782. In 1778 it was proposed to add board and continuous supervision as hitherto a limited !num- ber of children had been clothed and educated only. To effect this most desirable object, a large outlay was necessary, as there was no building in War- rington suitable for the purpose. A special subscrip- tion was entered into, headed by Mr. John Black- burn, and followed by other trustees and their friends, and the sum of £2,000 was soon available for the purpose of erecting new buildings. The dawn of 178'2 saw the new school opened under the name of "The Warrington Blue Coat Hospital." The first master was Mr. John Webster,of Liverpool. As a result of the change, twenty-four boys and six girls were boarded, lodged, and educated, and on attaining the age of fourteen years received, as an apprentice fee, a gratuity of .£2. Six of these children were se'ected from the pupils of the old charity school, and the remainder from the town generally. It will be interesting to notice that the children were then one half the day in school, and the other half engaged in industrial occupations, chiefly weaving. One of the most munificent benefactors was "Honest John Watkins," as he was styled, and who we.- engaged in the business of smelting copper from the ore at Bank Quay. In 1802 want of funds com- pelled the trustees to close the school but two years afterwards it was opened as a day school only and remained so for twelve years under the master- ship of Mr. Bullock, of Shrewsbury. In 1814 the old plan of taking the children into the house was reverted to and it was decided to continue the oay school also. Mr. John Elorrocks, of Lowton, suc- ceeded Mr. Bullock, and the aohool was conducted henceforward on the "Madras oyatem." In 1832 the Act of Parliament, 2nd and 3rti William IV., was obtained, which now regulates the csarity and Mr. and Mrs. Forster were appointed master and mis- tress in 1835. Mr. Bowes was appointed to the office on the death of Mr. Forster in 1852 and held it until his death in 1882, when Mr. Itose, the present master, succeeded him. Duriug the time Mr. Bowes was master of the Blue Coat School James Kendrick, M.D , honorary medical examiner to the institution, made charges of neglect and abase against the trustees towards the children and resigned his connection with the institution. Dr. Kendrick attributed the evils he exposed principally to the fact that the Blue Coat Scnool Trustees wee" strongly and undeniably of one political and often hereditary bias." They were Tories and it is worthy of note that the Doctor him- self was a Tory. However, with the truth or the contrary of these accusations we have nothing to do, further than that they had their effect and certain things were remedied. That is in brief the history of the Warrington Blue Coat School. An interesting tact, though not a surprising one as Warrington can boast of many old families, is Vast many of the present trustees are relatives of previous benefactors. he building now shelters 57 children; 33 boys, and 24 girls whose bright, healthy looks are sufficient guarantee for the benefit they obtain in, and the pleasure they derive from their quarters. How many city or town children we wonder, whose lives are simply existence, would envy them their places did they but se them? The comfortable little chapel was one of the first places I visited. It is well lighted,

fitted with comfo-rtable seats and a substantial look- ing stove gave promise that the youngsters and , their visitors would not feel the cold during the winter months. A new two manual pedal organ has , hot long since been substituted in place of the old one which had done duty from a period soon after the Institution was built. A stained glass window on which was the following, bore tribute to the memory of cue whom many IVarriugtoniaus will remember :—" R. B. Edmundsou & Son, stainers, Warrington, 1546." In the bedrooms, eich boy or girl in the establishment is represented by a little cot at the bottom of which each one has a locker, so that there is no confusion. At one time wardrobes were used, but the idea suggested itself to Mr. Rose that by fitting a locker at the bottom of each bed, the bedroom used as a wardrobe could be used for Eome other purpose. This suggestion was carried

into effect, and now saves miin-11 confusion. Each is provided with a separate comb and brush so that the little ones are quite independent of each other for such daily .necessities. Not a speck of dust could be seen in the rooms, and everything was in perfect order. Each scholar in the Institu- tion has to make his or her own bed, and in fact all the work in connection with the place is done by the inmates. One room fitted with two beds is ecially arranged for isolating doubtful cases of sickness or children taken with the measles. Six excellent baths were fitted up when the place was enlarged some years ago. What is now used as the sewing room was at one time the dining room but this was Lund too small when the number of chil- dren increased and so a dining room was built and the old dining room relegated to that very necessary part of the work, in view of the fact that all the girls' clothes and all the boys' underclothing is made on the premises, sewing. What will immediately attract tile visitor on entering the room are a num- ber of prints by Hogarth—original ones, not copies—entitled " The Industrious and Idle Apprentices," the set of twelve being presented to the iustitution by Dr. Muir, " An old Blew," some 12 years ago. I was not surprised to find in this room aho, some oak chests whizh wouid make

many a person inclieed to break a commaadment by being covetoue. Wite the heating arrangements in the back kitchen, Mr. Rose said they were able to get about 20 barns heated in an hour and a half. A. visit to the washhoueese which are also under the care of the girls and lad: gaave ins an opportunity of seeing a Blue Cat School " washing day," and unlike many households, they are quite independent of the weather for- drying purposes as a room heated by steam, fel- which the b)ys are responsib:e, is utilised when the weather is not favourable• The play groends were the next place: we visited, and here we found the children indulging in games and happy as larks. The playgrounds are excel- lently fitted with apparatus for providing complete exercise and enjeyinent and in triewer to a remark from Mr. Rose who displayed his natural pride in their cempletertess, 'admitted they would compare favourably 'with the best in Warriugton. The children, who are under the care of two male teackers in addition to Mr. Rose, rise at six o'clock in a morning, and breakfast at 7.30. The school hour are from 3 to 12 and from 2 o'clock until 4.30,a1l retiring to bed at eight o'clock. From this one can see that with regular hours for sleeping and school, and plenty of exercise and good food, the children under the kindly discipline of Mr. Rose lead very healthy lives. In addition to the ordinary elementary subjects, shorthand and typewriting are now taught, the latter being insti- tuted last yeareso that those who have a bent for a bueiness life are excellently fitted for the same. Tne girls are also, fram their responsibility for household affaire,thoroughly treined,and make good domestic servants. The boys leave the Institution at 14, and th 3 girls at 10, and each one is provided at the time witti a complete outfit. No better testi- mony to the care and training the boys and girls receive at the Blue Coat School could be advanced than the fact that so many of our citiz3ns—it is needless to mentioe names as they are so well- known—occupying positions of trust, and profes- sional men, have been brought up there, and, I may add, they are only too proud ti acknowledge the fact. After the inquiry held at the Town Hall last year into the Warrington Charities, the Charity Commis,ioner paid a visit to the School and expressed himself as highly pleased with the arrangements for the welfare of the children. The history of the Blue Coat School is so intimately associated with the history of Warrington that it is to be devoutly hoped that so lone as Warring- ton occupies a place on the map of Enelend, the Blue Coat School will flourish, and we need have no fear that the Institution will not continue to flourish so long as the Board of Trustee; is composed of such gentlemen as the present Board includes : men who have the interests of the youngsters at heart, as evidenced by their thoughtfulness in omitting nothing that will tend to make them good citizens and useful members of society.

div.head: FIRST ENGLISHMAN TO BE CURED OF TUBERCULAR CONSUMPTION.
div.p: THE FIRST ENGLISHMAN TO BE CURED OF TUBERCULAR CONSUMPTION.
A LADY'S BENEFICENCE.

Within a gunshot of th'l Drake memorial at Taxis- tock are monumental stone works, where works a young man, twenty-seven years of age, who is as active as any of his fellow toilers. Yet no more than a year ago be lay in a helpless and hopeless condition in bed, having been discharged from the Tivistock Cottage Hospital a incurable. Interviewed by a representative of the " Tavistock Gazate," he made the following state- ment

'My ovne is John Giles Rogers, and I am a monu- mental mason. I was taken seriously ill at the age of 24. A diseaaed bone in the foot eves the commencement of nil illness, which was general tuberculosis. I went to the South Devon and East Cornwall Hospital, Ply- mouth, where I remained under treatment for six weeks. At the end of the six weeks I earns out of the hospital, although icy foot was not thoroughly healed. I went to work, and continued at my avocation by dint of great effort for three months. In the meantime I had been gradually losing lissh, me appetite was gone, I grew weaker every day, and at last was confined to my bed, suffering from general and increasing denility. There I remained for seven weeks, and then I was ad- mitted to theiTavistock Cottage Hospital,whero I stayed for three months. I was treated there with the greatest kindness, and I believe that every effort was made to improve my health, but without avail, and I was dis- charged as incurable, with tuberculosis. " My friends were informed that noaling more could be done for me,and that I had net long to live. I had a severe pain in the back, was short of breath, and could only crawl along. I never expected to go to work again and everyone knew that I had the fatal tubercular form of consumption. The weakness of the spine and general debility increased to such an extent that I had to re- main in bed again, and this time I thought that it was ' all up with me. One day, while glancing at the paper in bed. I read of a case of consumption, .which was stated to have beets cured by Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people. A. lady had kindly promised to do anything she could tor me, so I sent the paper by my wile to this lady, who after reading the ankle, gave her money to purcnase a box of the pills. I took one after each principal meal— three a day—And after five days I was able to get out of bed. The pills produced an invigorating effect and thoroughly braceu me op. 'Two days later I was walking about the town. I took five boxes of Dr. Williams' pink pills altogether, and kept gainieg strength. That was ten months ago. Since Cita I have never lost an hour, but have regularly worked from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m.—ten hours a day. I have a good appetite, and am perfectly well." Tnc ca.e of Mr. Rogers is remarkable, an he is the first man in England to be cured of tubercular consumption —hithert, regarded as incurable. The other form of consumption (marked by blood-spitting and night sweat) haa many times been cure i by Dr. Williams' pink pills, which act directly en the blood. Lack of blood is the direct cause of physical and functional weakness, neadachee, palpitation et the heart and painful breathlessness after exertion, backaches, cold feet, and the general wretchedness of " delicate " people. 'the special troubles ot girls in their development nearly always arise from anfenais. ; in popular language, front " too little blood ;" and Dr. llrilliarns' pink pills cure all .the consequences of that manner in a lack of spoken of as miraculous.
