THE REV. E. R. TARRUCK AND SUNDAY TRADING. _ _

Preachioe in St. Paul's Church, on Sunday morning, on the question of Suedav trading, the Rev. E. R. Tarback. vicar, observed thet competition was sole:ring iu its keenness ; it was getting harder, although it was quite hard enough now. Competition a short time ago suer:rested to two of the London newspapers that they I should, in order to return a better interest on the eapitat ' tat bad been laid on teem, have Sunday editions. These editions were subsequently started and the nation was rou'oei. The" Daily Mail" was the first of the two papers to announce that it wonld give up the Sunday • edidons, and it gave as one of its strongest reasons for ladopting that course that it had received a petition from , its own staff who were perFeetly loyal to the owners,but at the same time, while thankine the roasters for their , consideration at all times, they felt bound in this case to utter the voice of protest. Another day in the week was offered them in the place of Sunday, but they pre- ferred the coesmon day for common worshin. That was a most important feet in the history of England. ! and they should feel very strongly that ti's first object for which God gave them :lie Sunday was for man's ' ' highest development—thtt they could not develop to the highest position unless they had a ' day of rest and worship. He was a strange kind of workiogrnaa who, after w:,rking 5i days ,or six days, ceild no on the sevente give thanks to God the rewarder of all toil. It was said that no one was harder on the workingman than the working-non himself ; It was possible he had been a little hard on him in the past, bat it had bsen rather because he had not I had the question explainet to him fully. Otherwise he I felt certain teat be %voted have net only juetice but ' mercy suflicient in his hart to see that no unfairness was ulaeed upo 4 his fello w- werk man in any way if he could avoid it. These who were most inelined to cause work to be done on a Sandey.ts prevent people joining in common prayer, were not the workers but tnese who "neither toil nor spin." In mercy to their fellow men , let them see that they did not in the slightest degree add to the amount of labeur regained on a &Imlay; let them not cause a single person to work a single m 'meat more than neeessary. Trips oa a Sunday were now being orgarezecl by the railway compeniee, not fes delicate people, hut for people who had every Saturday after- noon at their disposal, and if they did not protest aeseust teas, stile of things, they would seen heye the Parisian Sunday in their midet. The number of shopkeepers who from worthy Or unworthy sessen3 were opening their doors on a Sunday was increasing. There were wily two kinds of shops at the met that hid any retsoa whatever for opening on a Su eley— me was the chemist and the other !he pabli- can. The Be is allowed them to eat on the S abbath Day. and if they had a omsteing to eat they weuld want something to drine. Be had made it his business to see several publicans during the last few weeks, and he bad found that there was a feeling amongst the licensed victuallers at any rate that they vrould like, like other peorils, a rest on a Sunday, and it would therefore, be a good thug if they could arrange to opsn from twelve to one and from five to six. Front a letter in the local Ipress, it appeared that the number of small deeps that were being opened on Sunday was increasing in War-. rington. Allusion was made to several tobacconists Ishops. He (Mfr. Tarbuck) contended that they were committing a great sin if they bought a pennyworth of sweets on a Sunday, a cigar, or an ounce of tabeceos They had all the week in which to buy these things, which were not periehable, and he would prefer them making these purchases as late as twelve o'clock on a Saturday night rather than do anything to encourage Sunday trading. CHRIST THE PRINCE OP PEACE. Mr. T. Rylance, of Pemberton, in iectering on the above subject on Sunday, iu the Christadelphian Room. Bold-street, pointed out the fact that before Christ ruled as the Prince of Peace he would come as a man of war and destroy his ene niee. To those who were sceptical as to Christ's ever coming to this earth again, he com- mended Christ's owes womb "If I go away, I will come again," and other similer promises. The lecturer, after referring to the time approaching, when God" should destroy them which destroy or corrupt the earth " quoted many passages of Scripture to show the glorious time which followed after evil was rooted out of the earth, and Christ the Prince ,if Peace was King over all the earth. Jeremiah told them that the Branch " Christ " should execnte judgment and justice its the earth, and toe promise which Christ gave His disciples in response to Peter's inquiry what they should have weo bad follewed him was net that they should go to heaven, but that they •shauld sit upon twelve threnes judging the twslve tribes of Israel when the Son of man shall sit in tbe throne of His glory and which time was mentioned in Revelation where tuo redeemed sang" We shall reign on the earth." The words so often said "Thy Kingdom come" had reference to this good time c ming when "The Lord would destroy the veil teat is spread over all nations" and when he " would turn to the people a pure language that they might all call upon the name of the Lord." There would then be no poor people in the earth, nor would there be any sorrow or sickness for unless the terms offered by God "belief, obedience, faithful" were accepted rules there would not be any chance of having a part in the ruiership of the world when Christ took to himself his great, power and reigned in the earth. —O.--. div.head: FUNSEAL.
div.p: FUNSEAL.

On Sunday afternoon—&-- remains of the lute Bugle-Major David rhiaston, whose lamentably suuden death was recorded in our. last issue, were interred with full military honours in the Cemetery The Volunteers assembled at the Dill Hall at half past twelve. Major Buckton was in command,aad there was a muster of about 200, including Captain Cnorley, Sergeaut-Major Rawlinson, Sergeant-In- structer Barker. and a full attendance of sergsants. They marched to the lute residence of the deceased in Buttermarket-estreet,where the funeral cortege was formed. A tiling party under Sergeant Ryder, the baud and buglers, and a large number ot representa- tives et the Order of Piresters (of which deceased was a member) preceded the hearse, which was followed by the private carriages, several m...mbers or the Licensed Victuallers' Association and the Volunteers. At the bottom of Buttermarket-street the funeral procession was joined by a number oE Sergeauts attached to the Bth and 40th Regimenta/ District. The route to toe cemetery was lined with spectators, and there was a large attendance of the general public at the cemetery. The demonstration was an e/oquent indication of the respect and es- teem in which the deceased gentleman was held. Tie chief mourners were Mrs. rlinston (widow), Mr J W Plinston, Miss Itaggie Pliuseon, and Messrs David, Edward, Frederick, Charles and Valentine and Miss Elizabeth Plinsten (sons and. (laugh:en), Mrs -1 W (daughter- in-law), Messrs William, Samuel, Edward and John Piinstou (b:othere), Mrs Beswick and. Mrs. Bradshaw (sisters), Mrs. William, Mrs Sumac). and Mrs I.uward Ylinston (sisters-in-law), Mrs. Walsh, Mr Dr.vid Beswick, mr Beswick, ;NAr Ernest Plinston, Mr iLdwin Plins- ton, .Mr James Walsh, Mr and Mrs J Charneck, Mr William Charucck (nephews and nieces), and Mr John Gandy (cousin). Among others present were Councrltor Rogers and M, ssrs. Turner, Massey, Tur- ley. Ruslaworta, McClinton, and Walsh (secretary), representing the Licensed Victuallers.' Association (Councillor 6h6lcock and Mr Jenks being prevented from attendieg);aud representatives irons the Order of Foresiers,the Amalgamated Society of Engineers. and the Arpley Cricket Ciub(ot which deceased was a vice-president). The funeral service, both in the chapel and at the graveside, was conducted by the Rev W II Thummood,Mikahe bearers were Colour- sergeants Woo:, Juiley, Spenc.:r, and Sergeants Brainhall, Davenport and Ward. The coffin, which was of polished oak with bass mountings, bore the following inscriifrcion : " David Flirts:Am, died June 16, Iti9o, aged 51 ears." At the couclusian of the servite at tee graveside one of toe forestels de- livered a brief address, the tiring party tired three volleys, and the bugler souaded the long reveille. The aervice throughout was of a most impressive character.

JUNE 23rd 1899.

THERE are some encouraging Signs of Political Movement. signs of political movement. The voting in South Edin- burgh, by its volume and its result, must have 11°1110 meaning. There is no great exultation tabout it the smith of the Tweed. There are some 'eelings about it north of that river. The Scotch People are getting about tired of that masquerade 4:4 Unionism which has had such disastrous effects 11Pon:the old representatives of that home of sturdy rociple and logical politics. Mr. DEWAR makes 4t as one of his strong points that Edinburgh has tebelled against the political paralysis which lies erePt over it since the better classes bowed the 'lee to Unionism as a new and a saving creed. If ' there are like indications in East Edinburgh we °ball hardly be unwise to see in them the agree- able signs of reaction. Scotland has had a pretty good spell of that unsatisfactory kind of political life which uses a name and enunciates general Principles, and then votes as if neither the name nor the principles were deserv- ing of honour. The good advice which fol- lows victory as well as disaster is to the effect that by-elections never have any value one waY or the other. We are familiar with the 841.1 If the majority for a Ministerialist be 'tkereased it is incontrovertible evidence that the er °vernment is still popular and still retains the eftfidence of the country, whereas if a member of The Opposition should win a seat it is always con" t4)oient to explain it by whims and mere personall katters. It is not in this way that the genera Public looks at events. It could not accept South- Port as an indication that the Government stood tlactly where it was, and it has not so regarded .c4cliaburgh. A much shrewder way of looking at ;vents is common, and it is perfectly justified. tillere must be some light and meaning in a big Y'election, especially when it takes place in the fleaPital of an important part of the United King- It cannot now be many days before we 3314 y have further evidence of movement. ; Lanca- tire has not been altogether well affected wards the Government, for very many eas°ns, including its attachment to Protestant- ea°3, and to Free-trade and the open door,or as the rlier expression used to be, "the open port "—a Zuell more accurate reading of a literal fact. ould the borough of Oldham prefer to return a iboral at the present juncture of affairs, we could Zat err in seeing in that fact a pregnant illustra- o° of the old saying that "what Lancashire

thinks to-day England thinks to-morrow." Accord- ing to the best evidence obtainable, such a result seems highly probable. If, on the other hand, 01(11-m:a should remain steadfast in its belief in the good qualities and deeds of the present Govern- ment, the general observer would certainly regard the fact, as possessing considerable significance. The fact is that we are looking out for the signs of the times, which are not to be found in Parlia- mentary debates and divisions by persons elected four years ago, but in the constituencies. We shall be guided to a logical conclusion by what these signs of movement are, and our judgment upon them must be influenced by the direction which they take.

LORD SALISBURY has an Commsrseioiniseleas? awkard way of darting across Ai the political horizon, at intervals, some flash of startling scepticism which leaves behind it hesitation, if not uncomfortable doubts and fears. His remarks about Royal Com- missions ought not to be in any deprecating or doubtful strain. He is the head of a Government which has appointed more Royal Commissions than any of which there is living recollection. If we have had our doubts at times of the motives which have animated the appointment, we have always been instructed to suspend legislative hopes and schemes until they had reported, the assump- tion being that as soon as they did report the Government would know what to do. When anyone suggested that Commissions were mere schemes for putting off, or for doing what SAM WELLER declared to be the chief aim of medicil practice "amusing the patient whilst nature performed the cure" —he was charged with being a narrow and a bigoted partisan. Now, we have Lord SALIS- BURY himself throwing a big cold douche on soma of his own Commissions. "I think I know several Commissions now pending that have not the slightest probability of any action being taken upon them." The peers laughed heartily. They were thinking of Lord PEEL'S Licensing Commis- sion, no doubt, and probably the remark had a pointed reference to the inquiry which has been 1 going on now for several years and has not yet officially reported. Was it, after all, a mere diver- siod, intended to keep the temperance party in- active, to soothe the minds of ardent Conservative reformers, and to shelve the question for years by making it so large that no one would venture to tackle it? Some of us have thought so, and we have been scoffed at. But here is Lord SALISBURY who, in the name of the appointing Govern ment, predicts that several Commissions still at work will command no further notice - whatever from his Government. A dash of cynicism marks the whole deliverance, and it is especially Salisburian. The noble PREMIER is a master of flouts and gibes. He and his friends cannot legislate until they have had elaborate inquiries, and so they propose them, to make us believe that they are intending to legis- late. Do not be deceived, Lord SALISBU RY says; some of our Commissions are mere intellectual and political exercises for the edification of per- sons who want views and information. They are not at all likely to form the basis for carefully considered legislative schemes. Automatic coup- lings were put into a Bill, and when there was a 1 big hubbub a Commission was appointed. It is just getting to work. Can it be said of this Com- mission that there is "not the slightest probability of any action being taken upon it ?" If ao,we seem to get a new glimpse into the processes of poli- tics, and to discover that there really is some dif- ference between the Conservatives, who appoint Commissions to check all legislation, and the , Liberals, who follow Commissions by Bills and do their best to carry them into law. The Royal Commission, at its best, is a devise for exploring a subject with a view to legislation. At its worst it is a mere trick, a bit of fireworks, a deliberate at- tempt to deceive the public. It has been reserved for Lord SALISBURY to enable us tosee that public money is to be spent in investigations in order that a Government in office shall not lose votes by attempting to legislate. A more frank gleam of Machiavellianism we have not had for many a day.

-Recent action of the Bar Council has quickened interest in the question of a barrister's responsibi- lity to his client. It is rather the exception than the rule for an eminent leader at the Bar to follow through the cases in which he is retained. A client reserves for himsel', at preat expens3, the services of a brilliant advocate, and often his solici- tor tells hint he is lucky if that advocate conducts the cross-examination or replies to an argument he has not heard. The client becomes indignant, and puts down the loss of the suit to the neglect of his counsel. Sometimes in his next essay he takes the precaution to secure an eminent junior as well es a distinguished 'leader, and the exper- ience may be still more disheartening. The work will be done by" relief" methods which secure hest results in physical employment such as navvies, but are seeniingly perilous to a mental grasp of a case. There is, however,another side to this question. The whole scheme of attack or de- fence, when counsel are really conscientious (and highly paid), is worked out in previous consulta- tions, and when the mind of the chief has illumi- nated that of his junior the latter, if he be cap- able, is nearly as good as his master for all the work except the cross-examination of the chief witnesses. It is a mistake to suppose that per- siflage counts for much. The summing-up by a judge cuts under forced arguments. A case often stands or falls by its line of treatment and the presentation of the evidence, and this scheme is generally laid down beforehand. Theßa.e Coun- cil has decided that when a barrister gives an undertaking to appear in a case, and does net do so at all, he should return his fee; but it is im- possible to go further than that. The return of briefs because a counsel could not see a case through would mean disastrous eleventh-hour in- strit ctio us.

Those whom business takei to the police ;;our`i see much Of the seamy side of life, but in course of time they get somewhat indifferent to it; yet an incident occurred at the Warrington Police Court the other day which would leave an impression on the most callous. Words fail to describe the con- dition of a prisoner who waq charged with the theft of a coat and vest from a shop in -Alrsey- strcet. Drink and other evils had done their worst, for though only a middle-aged man he was a pitiable wreck of humanity. The police with a delicacy of feeling that did them infinite credit, rc • frained from making an exhibition of the man by bringing him into the COUTft Room before his trial. When the prisoner did make his appearance from the cells below, then to those persons with fine feelings,. the spectacle he made produced some- thing akin to a physical shock. The man, in answer to Tr stions from the Bench, and with or sional interraptions of laughter fzom specta- trs, related the story of 11:.s wanderings in an apathetic manner, which immediately changed when the Chairman asked him if he could dririk a glass of beer. His ready answer was: " Ave, twe," the humour of which evidently tickled the fancies of his audience. There is a facetious side to most things and we do well to appreciate it, but in the name of common humanity let us not laugh when our better nature bids us pity.
There were several subjects of more than ordinary interest under discussion at the Provin- cial Assembly of Presbyterian and Unitarian

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY JUNE 23, 1899.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY JUNE 23, 1899.

ministers and congregations of Lancashire and Cheshire held at Warrington last Thursday. We have become so familiar with the present contro- versy in the Church of England, known as the crisis in the church, that one really wonders whether anything fresh can be said on the subject. But we are yet only at the beginning of the con- troversy, and where it Fill end it is difficult to forecast. In the very thoughtful address from the chair Mr. Alderman Rawson, of Manchester, pointed out what is becoming more and more evident every day, that if the priestly party suc- ceed in the Church of England, disestablishment must inevitably follow. There are many extreme Ritualists who would welcome even this but who at the same time would scout any idea of disendowment. They are desirous of retaining the emoluments and enjoying the social prestige of the National Church, as the Chairman well said, but wish to insist on their personal interpre- tation of its rubric. It is around this knotty point of disendowment that the fight will grow keener, and Nonconformists of every name will have to unite their forces if they are to secure disendow- ment with disestablishment.

At an assembly of Unitarians it was perhaps only natural that a reference should be made to the statements which have been published recently that Unitarianism is a dying cause. The Rev. W. Harrison, of Stalybridge, dealt very ably with this subject in his discourse at the morning service. He showed that the criticism was based upon a wrong assumpti®n as to the position of Unitarian- ism. It existed not merely to destroy all that was destroyable in the orthodox system, but it existed to fulfil. F6W will deny that 'Unitarianism has done a great deal to rid orthodox teaching of much that was gross and erroneous, and that there still remains something to do in this connection. But 17nitarianism stands for something more than a mere protest, and this is, according to the preacher, " the unadulterated religion of Christ."

tBY A CORRESPONDRNT.] The appointment of Mr. George F. Ashton as clerk to tne Runcorn Union and Rural District Council, which was so unanimously conferred upon him Ache respectivl meetlugs of those bodies on Tuesday last, is one universally approved. It is simply the confirmation of the people's wishes and a decidedly popular appointment in every respect. Far many years Mr. George F. Ashton has acted as deputy to his late lamented father (Colonel John Ashton) and under him has undoubtedly received the finest possible training to fit him for the duties. During the time he filled the deputy post,and upon those tew occasions when in his father's latter years he has been called upon to fill the senior position, the ability and tact shown by him was ever the theme of high compliment; and that those compli- ments have been sincere was manifested on Tues- day by his unanimous appointment to the vacant offices. Mr. George Ashton is to be congratulated, and the appointment is accompanied by every good wish that he may live to enjoy the position which all feel he will fill with honour.

The Directors have settled the question as to whether or not the Camden Soap Works should go over to Widnes ; and, that too, in a way satisfac- tory to Runcorn people. as they have decided to retain the present site. But that is not the only gratifying feature. Not only will the works remain, but increased plant will be laid down, and exten- sions made in several departments. The decision of the directors confirms my remarks of some weeks ago, when I contradicted the rumour of their removal.

Lord John Sanger's Circus was the centre of at- traction on Wednesday and at both the perform- ances large crowds assembled to witness a most unique performance. The match arranged between S. Houghton and the goal-kicking elephant did not come off however. But whether it was owing to the elephant funking the redoubtable Sammy none can say, still if that was the case the poor beast need not be ashatnel for he's not the first to have a wholesome re;pect for the Runcorn full back. The dis.ppointment was somewhat allayed by the successful display of a young man named Ackerley who faced the huge carcase and managed to score a goal.

The drought has broken and during the week rain has fallen heavily. On Tuesday night a severe thunder-storm passed over the district, lasting some five-and-twenty minutes. The lightning was most vivid and the thunder exceedingly loud. As yet no damage to property has been reported ia the neighbourhood.

Throughout the district harvesting operations are being commenced, and during last week there was a great influx of the sons of Erin who, like the swallow, come as harbingers of summer. From general appearances the hay crops seem to be pretty solid, healthy, and abundant, a condition due no doubt to the heavy rains during the spring. On the condition of roots and cereals it is, however, too early to speculate.

An alarm of fire was raised at about 8 o'clock on Mon- day night, the conflagration having biokon out at the Globe Chemical Works, Widnes. The fire brigade turned out under assistant superintendent Franklin, and 50111 had a couple of hose playing on the burning parts. The re hid originated in a sulphur and charcoal shed, through the roof of which fl .mes were seen to be is;uin,.. The efforts of the firemen met with complete success,for in about half-an-hour the conflagration was got under, and the danger was at an end. The position was a serious one, for chemicsls of a highly explosive nature are manufactured in the works. This is the seconi fire which has occurred within a week at this pace. Super- inteudent Keighley andlnspector Strickland were in at- tendance with a body of police, and reniered valuable ass:stance in keeping back the large crowd which had assembled, notwithstanding the dangcrous nature of the outbreak. The cause of the fire is unknown, and tha amount of damage done is but slight.

THE CLERKSHIP.

The Chairman said toe comm-.;1-,e-e a.ppoin!T-1 t c-n- -eider the salary of the clerk had met that morninz and there WILSI a full atnodance. There wc•re only tw appointments the committee could deal with and one was the appointment of clerk to the Board of Guardians and the other was tke appointment of the clerk to the District Council. The School Attendance Committee and the Assessment Committee appointed their own clerk.
Mr. Linaker : That is not so. The Clerk to the Gull-- dialog is clerk to these committees, but the committees fixed the amount of remuneration.

Mr. Knowles said the committee had compared the salary of the late clerk with the salaries paid by other Boards of Guardians in Cheshire and one or two outside arid the committee unanimously recommended that the salary be reduced from £l.lO to £lOO. He moved the acceptance of the recommendation. Mr. Unaker seconded, and observed that the commit- tee fully considered the matter and thought £lOO a fair salary, including removals. The recernmendation was adopted. Mr. Woodward now moved the resolution of which he had given notice. The prospective Clerk of the Board needed no words of commendation freee him. The members all knew him, perhaps not quite so intimately as he did, b.cause as Chairman of the Finance Committee he had hien thrown into con- tact witn him a very great deal, and the more he knew him, the more convinced he was that Mr. George F Ash- ten was a very fit and proper person to occupy the poei- tion of Clerk to the Guardians. He looked upon Mr. Ashton as a very worthy and promisingyoung man, and he propoiei that, he be appointed clerk at a salary of £lOO per annum, with the understanding that he saall devote the whole of his time to the duties of the Union and Distric" Council, but that be should be allowed to pursue his seidies, with a view to qualifying himself for thel.gal profession, the earlier steps of which be had already taken. Mr. Wright seconded the motion, and said the Board could not have fixed upon a more suitable person than Mr, George Ashton. He had had a splendid training under his lather and at that Board of Guardians. Like Mr. Woodward be (Mr. Wright) had known much of Mr. Ashton because of his position on the Finince Committee. He had never been to Mr. A‘hton's office to make inquiries in connection with the Finance with- out him being in a position to give every information. He had not said " I will look it up "or anything of that kind. The Board were very lucky in having such a young man, who lead not to be taught his duties, to appoint. Mr. Linaker supported the proposition. He had some knowledge of the dude,' required by a person filling the office and he thought Mr. George Astitou would mike a very efficient clerk, During seine conversation Mr. Woodward said be thought the restriction in the appointment would be an inducement to Mr. Ashton to pursue his legal duties and thus extend his borders.
Tha motion was uhanimously adoptel,and Mr. George Ashton who had retired, was re-called inta the room and acqulinted by the Claairmah with the Board's deci- sion.

The newly-appointed Clerk said he thanked the mem- bers very much for the gr)at confiience they had placed in him by appaintinz him clerk, and especially was he crateful for the very kind way in which it bad been done. He should always do his utmost to deserve their confidence, and he booed hy faithfulness to all the duties of the office that in time he might have that gcod feeling borne to him that be knew was borne to his father. (Hear, hear). div.head: RUNCORN NATIONAL SCHOOLS.
div.p: RUNCORN NATIONAL SCHOOLS.

THE VICAR ON RELIGIOUS EDUCATION. On Sunday the annual sermons in behalf of the Run- corn National Schools were preached at the Parish Church. The merning preacher was the Rev F E Powell M.A., vicar of St. James's, Latchford, who preached an impressive sermon on religious education. In the after- noon a flower service was held, at which an appropriate address was delivered by the Rev E S Oliver, 8.8. The scholars contributed baskets and bouquets of flowers,to be afterwards distributed among the sick poor of the parish. At evensong there was a large congregation, notwithstanding the unfavotirable elements. The Vicar occupied the pulpit, and preached from the text : "The Lord bath called the child " (Samuel iii. 8). In the course of his sermon the reverend gentleman said they considered it was desirable to maintain their voluntary schools because they gave religious instruction. They were told very often that in board schools there was relizeous education. That was true of some board 1 schools, and it they inquired they would find that the religious instruction was left to the teachers. If they went a little further, and a: ked why did the teachers wish to give religious instruction in board sshools, they would find, if they followed the history of those teachers, that they were trained in voluntary schools. There they were surrounded by religious instruction, and when they went to the training colleges, which belonged to the different denominations of Christians, they were still surrounded by religious instruction. After that they very likely went into a voluntary school, thus it was that the religious instruction given in some boar d sehoels was really due to the voluntary system. In ceeclusion, Canon Wood said, supposing a man was rated at LIO a year, if their voluntary schools in Runcorn were closed, and others built to supply the recriirements of the town, it would cost him 8s a year. That man was, therefore. 8s a year better off than he would be because of the existence of these schools. He appealed to them to make some little self-denial, and to give liberally in the offertory. During the service the choir gave an admirable rendering of the anthem, " Wherewithal shall a young man" (Sir G. Elvey), the solo part being well sustained by Mr. W. E. Dudley. The services were also given a festive character by the singing of processional and recessional hymns.

div.head: ANOTHER SHOCKING SUICIDE AT FRODSHAM.
div.p: ANOTHER SHOCKING SUICIDE AT FRODSHAM.

Oa Thursday morning the po!ice received intelligence of another shocking suicide by drowning in the River Weaver Canal. .The rash act was committed by Samuel Burkhill, labourer of Bridge-lane, Froishana. Bnrkhill who was employed by Messrs. Ashworth, Limited, left off work about six o'clock on Thursday morning. He went borne as usual taking his can and basket with him. About seven o'clock his daughter got up and not seeing anything of her father about the place, and noticing that he had left his watch in the house, she raised an alarm aud requested some of her neighbours to searci for her father. Several joined in the search and eventu- ally some of his clothing was found on the canal side by two young men named Joseph Cord well, and Thomas Roughsedge. The police were informed and Constable Price securing a.,sistance dragged the canal with the re- sult that about 10-30 the missing man's body was re- covered As the man's fee: were tied together there can be little doubt that deceased committed suicide. An inquest will probably be held to-day (Friday.)

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES.
A FRODSHAM MAN BEFORE THE WARRINGTON M AG ISTRAT F. 3 .

At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Tuesday before Messrs. Garnett kin the chair) and Guest, a miserable-looking, middle-aged, and badly-dressed man, named Daniel Frodsham. described " as last from Man- chester and a native of Frodaham," was charged with having on the previous afternoon stolen from the shop of Mr. Gibbons, Mersey-street, a jacket and vest, of the value of 10s. 6d.—When asked to plead, prisoner replied ' "Any road svill do."—The Chief Constable said that the ' complainant was a second-hand clothes dealer, who I lived a few doors below his shop. He was standing at his private door at 20 minutes past two, when he saw the prisoner deliberately steal the jacket and vest and walk quietly away down the street with them. Mr. Gibbocs followed the man and gave him into the cus- tody of Detective Forster. When charged with the offence at the Police Station Frodaham replied 'lt won't kill me, this won't." Mr. Talbot added that the prisoner had been travelling about the country for the past ten years. He had just come out of gaol, where he had teen many times for begging and thieving. The man was a human wreck.—Prisoner : My right hand is paralyzed.—The Chief Constable : I don't know how long it is since he was washed, but I could quite believe him however long ho might say it was.—Prisoner : Several week.—The Chairman : When did you come from Manchester P—Prisoner : The day before yesterday.—What for ?—I was going to Frodtham.—Did you ever know •‘ Tommy from Frodsham 2—Yes sir 2—Where is he 2—l don't know. I think he is dead.—Was he related to you ? No sir.—What part of Frodsham , did you live in ? Opposite the Police Station. (Laughter.)—Have you any relatives there 2—Yes.—How long is it since you saw them 2—About ten vears.—They would be pleased to see you by this time I should think. (Laught-r.)—l have seen nothing of them for about 12 years.—Mr. Guest :—Have you done any work ?—I cannot do any— How long is it since you worked ?—About five years.— The Chief Constable: He told me ten yesterday. I don't think the man's hand is paralysed. I think it is stiff from want of USB.—Tho Chairman: Could you drink a glass of beer if it were put before you? —Prisoner (promptly): Aye, two. (Lend Ilaughter.)— Further questioned, the man said he had been an inmate ofputton Workitouse.—Mr. Gibbons said he felt sorry for the poor fellow, and he did not wish to press the case against him. He had before the robbery given the man some bread and butter and told him to go away, as he might get into trouble.—The Bench decided to record a conviction against the prisoner and allow hint to go, the Chairman telling him "to get a good wash as it was a long time since he bad seen water."—Prisoner : I don't bother myself about water. (Langhter.)—Fle then left the court. BROTHERS IN AFFLICTION SENT TO PRISON. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Tuesday morning, before Messrs. R. Garnett (in the chair) and E J. Guest,two powerfully built men, with b idly scratched faces, named George Hopkins and James Hopkins, brothers, of 15, Melville-street, were charged with hav- ing been drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street on the previous night and assaulting John Hatton, barman at the Lion Hotel Vaults, Bridge-street. George was further charged with breaking an ornamental glass deer at twenty minutes to eleven, doing damage to the ex- tent of £3.—John flatton, the barman, said the pri- soners came intothe house at 10.30. George asked him for a gill of beer, but be refused to serve him, and this BO annoyed him that he went into another compartment spoke to a man who was there,and commenced to create a disturbance. He told him to leave, but he refused to do go. Witness went towards the man to eject him when he deliberately broke the window either with his fist or his elbow. The glass was 3ft. Bin. by 2fl. flin.—By the Chief Constable : The man was not pushed through the wiadow. Witness detained the men until the arrival of the police. The prisoner George tried to bite him, and during the struggle which followed both fell to the floor. The other prisoner asked him to liberAs his brother,and because he would not do so he commenced to kick wit- ness, whose body was very much swollen. When the men were taken into custody they were very rough and made use of disgusting language. None of the :nen had bad drink in the house.— James Hopkins: We had drink nowhere else.—Jonathan Hayes, the manager, said prisoner James was having " argument" with another man. He went to quell the bother when" smash goes the window." (Laugh- ter.) He saw the barman on the floor, he was being assaulted by the prisoners. Neither of the men had had any drink in the house. He had previously given in- structions that they should not be served —George Hopkins said he and his brother had a pint of drink in the vaults. They were there nearly four hours.—The Chief Constable : Tee last time they were here they made the same remark abmt another house.— Sergeant Dean corroborated, and, said he had to nearly " throttle " one of the prisoners to get hint off Hatton. —P.C. Reddington also gave evidence.—The Chief Con- stable said that George had been before the magis'rates 44- times for various offences and Jame: 24 times. The men were note rious characters, and a great nuieance in the town. They were a, terror to publioans.—The Chairman : The publican's trade is a trade which is conducted under difficult conditions, and it is brought about by such men as the prisoners. The decision of the Court is that George be sent to prison for tbree months with hard labour and James for one month.

SMART CAPTURE BY THE WARRINGTON POLICE. On Tuesday the occasion of the visit of NIL John Sanger's circus to this town the Warrington police achieved a smart capture for which they deserve every credit.' A. man named John Twigg,who formerly lived at Warrington, but who left it fifteen or six- teen years ago,was wanted by the Salford police on a charge ot embezzlement in 1897. Searching in- quiries were made,but with no result until Tuesday when Superintendent Monaghan and Detective Forster were in the neighbourhood of Singer's show. The Superintendent had some knowledge ot Twigg. but the latter had greatly altered. He was employed at the show, and Superintendent Mona- ghan on seeing him went to him, spoke to him calling him by name, and telling him he Was wanted for a litte affair at Salford. Twigg at first denied being the man, but afterwards admitted itt He was taken to the police station and locked up. On Tuesday night he was taken in custody to Sal- ford in charge of Detective-eergeont Dillou, of the police force of that town. PRINTS AND MUSLIMS. W. T. PR—E-8-ENTATIoN AT Sr. PAUL'S SUNDAY SCHOOL. A very pleasing function was performed on Sun- day in connection with St. Paul's Sunday school. Mr. J. Lawless has been superintendent of the girls' department for nearly a quarter of a century, but, owing to ill health, he has been strongly urged by the doctor to give up all work on Sundays. This fact becoming known to the Vicar (Rev. E. R. Tar- buck), it was decided to raise funds for a testi- monial to Mr Lawless, wbich last Sunday was pre- sented in the form of an illuminated address and a purse at gold. There was scarcely standing room for those who came in from the other schools to wish Mr Lawless farewell. The address,which was executed free of charge by Mr Percy Aukland, was designed with exquisite taste, and will form a very pretty memorial for Mr Lawless to hand down to his children. Amongst those present, besides the Vicar and Mrs Tarbuck, were the Rev H V Pigot, the Rev li A Lester, Miss Lawless and Itif,B Rirarner,Messrs A J Jolley (boys' school superintendent),lV Chantry (vicar's warden). J H Smethurst, J T Bate, and C II Hamilton. The Vicar made the presentation, and alluding in feeling terms to the long period of hard and enthusiastic work done by Mr. Lawless, and expressed a hearty hope that the recipient of the testimonial might improve in health and be spared many years of usefulness. Mr. Pigot expressed his deep appreciation of his eight years' comradeship with Mr. Lawless in the work of the Sunday schools. Mr. Lawless, who was 6eeply affected,said he hoped those present would excuse him if his remarks were not adequate to the occasion, but this was a severance from work which he had loved and taken a pride in, and he was only sorry that his poor health prevented its continuance. Mr. Lawess's favourite hymn, "For ever with the Lord," was then sung most heartily by the children, and the proceedings concluded with the blessing.

A FORGIVING WlFE.—dstherine Palin summoned Thomas Josiah Palin for assaulting her on the sth inst.—Whan the case was called on the complainant said she wished to with- draw the summons as defendant had promised to treat her better. She appeared in the box with a black eye.—The Chairman addressing the defendant, said it was a cowardly thing for a man to assault his wife. Had not she begged him off it would have gone hard with him. Why didn't he fight a man his own size. The bench assented to the cue being withdrawn.

A liCENE AMONG3T THE Safer.,-33.—Sarah Sadler WAS charged with using abusive language towards Mary Ann Safler, whereby a breach of the peace might have been occa- sioned on the 15th June.—Mary Ann Sadler was also sum- moned by Sarah Sadler for the same offence.—Mr. Knowles, of Widnes, who appeared for Sarah Sadler steted that the parties e telt married a man of the name of Sadler, whom, he believed, worked at the same works.—Complainant stated that she lived at 26, Pickove-st., Muni:lora, and kept a ohip potatoe shop. Her husband wits a labourer at the Salt Works. On the 15th inst. witness was standing at. her door speaking to a neighbour, when the defendaat, Sarah Sadler. came past. BOWLING.
LANCASHIRE v. YORKSHIRE.

After an interval of a couple of seasons, the engage- ment between these two counties was resumed on Saturday at Chapeltown. near Leeds. The green is one of the most ancient in the county, and is about as intri- cate and full of " music " as the most ardent trundler could desire. The opening round proved a little die- couraging to the visitors, who, after the first four games had dropped about two dozen shots. In this slaughter the 'visiting president end vice-president with two able helpmates suffered. estwell, of Newton-le-Willows, past-champion, completed the first win for Lancashire by putting in a couple for game after a well-fought bat- tle. Wilson, of the Manchester Scottish, was also suc- cessful, and the two reduced the adverse majority to half. Two gains and a loss for the visitors left the score in about the same condition, but a rue-sway event in which the Yorkshire champion dismissed an experienced Broughton bowler for the heavy number of 16 shots sent the home side far ahead and shook the confidence of Lancashire in the playing strength of their team. Soon altnrwards the amateur champion of 1858 and the ex-champion of 1895 were distanced for totals of nine and eleven respectively. Results that were to seme'extent recovered by the play of the two Isherwoods, of Leigh and Radcliffe respectivelv. Chappell. of Lower Broughton, trundled very success- fully against Stead. of Spero Valley, and Jones, of Bar- purhey, earned the honour of distancing a Yorkshireman at a single figure return, the only instance of the kind during the engagement. The representatives of Prest- wich fared but poorly in the encounter, the two falling for a total of 15 points. Turnbull, of Radcliffe. and Jones, of North Warrington, were both successful against their opponents. but Lancashire suffered a most unlooked-for loss ist the return of W. W. Wells, generally admitted one of the mast accomplished players in the county. The majority against the visitors gradually increased, and by the time all the competitors had carried their woods off the turf Yorkshire e-al found to have 46 shots in hand to add to their score at Old Trafford on the 28th July. div.head: WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCLETY.
div.p: WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCLETY.
ANNUAL MEETING

The me.eting on Sunday of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society was dev.ited almost cx..ilusively to ba,ihess. Tele chair was cy.icupied by the presidar, (Rev. J. Yong') and he was supported by the officers of the sec;ecy. After de- votional exercises, the presideut delivered a short ad- dress to the members. He said their numbers were not so large a.; they were a few years ago, but they must not let this discourage them. He for one did not think t'neir work was geing to fail. Thy had sufficient evidence to encourage them to believe that the work they were doing was being blesaed of God. Homes were being brightened,and lives of men were be- ing lifted up, and beuefit,.ed in ways more thin they could tell. They must put all their energies into the work during thq present year, and see if they could net. decese some 'means of increasing their membership. Although there were other meetings of a similar kind held in the town, still the fact faced them that there werelarge numbers of men who did not make a practice of attending any place of worship, and who would be all the better for attending a P.S.A. meeting. It was a painful thing; to see large numbers of men c;ming ou;', of public-'inuses at closing times on Sun:lay. The P.S.A. was started as a missionary enterprise to endeavour to reach men who did not attend any place of worship. 'rhos, had succeeded to a great extent, but there was still much to be done, and they might expect their P.S.A. to flourish if they wakened up, and took their share, in making it known, and recruiting its ranks.
THE SECRETARY'S REPORT.

Mr. THOMAS WALLINGTON (the hon secretary), then read tne antiusl report. He said he felt proud to sub- mit the 6 h annual report. As they looked back and recalled to mind the events of another year he thought they would agree that it was filled with much joy and helpfulness; j ,y because of the continued presence of so many at the meetings, and helpfulness derived from the manly words of counsel and advice given by thom who had come to speak to them. While admitting that the attendances were not as larze as they would have liked to se, yet they had every reason to toe proud that so many came week by week, and he for one was de- lighted to report on the good work done during the sixth year of their society, which at one time was voted by some as an institution that would not survive its first year. They must bear in mind that others had followed their example of holding P.S.A. meetings for men in the town and district, and in one place the least expected awl the most surprising:. These societies must have an effect upon their P.S.A. Society. They hoped and prayed that these societies would be a source of blessing and help to all who attended the meetings, and that the districts wherein they were working, made all the better by their influence. The year closed with an enrolled membership of 770. The year previous ended with 905 so that they were 135 less. The number sim- ply stood for the actual number of members cards issued, and included a gaodly number who took out membership cards and who lapsed after meking only a. few attendances. The average weekly attend- ance of both members and non-members had been about 450. 851 books were gained as prizes during the year, 437 for the first six months and 414 for the second, mad these added to the number of prize books gained for the five years previous made up a grand total of 6,505. (Hear, hear.) Some mem- bers he was sorry to say,adopted the doubtfnl procedure of paying up for beck weeks 80 as to be entitled to their prize. It was hardly fair to those %she scarcely missed a meeting during the year, as they got the same kind of a book in value and yet proleably had been away for 12 or 13 weeks. The committee during the year undertook a general visiting scheme of the whole membership. This work was very faithfully carried out by the visitors,and although it did not affect their attendances very materially, yet it must have done a great amount of good, and probably the Society might reap a behefit therefrom in the future. During the year there was inaugurated a sick club, and which, he was pleased to say, had been a decided success. He should like to press its advantages, and plead that the member- ship (which at present numbered about 90) might be added to, so that they mieht have amongst them a large number providing for themselves for times of need. Whilst providing for the future, let them not forget the benevolent fund which had done so much good in its time. They were again greatly indeb- ted to all whc helped them in the working of the society. The number enrolled so far in the present year was 497, and they were naturally looking forward to that num- ber being considerably augmented. He would plead with those who had reaped so much bele!, and benefit from attending its meetings, ts, let others know of those blessings, to lend a helping hand in the work, to speak and pray fer the society that it might still continue in the great work of the Master, and adding souls to His Kingdom.

div.head: BENEVOLENT AND SICK FUNDS.
div.p: BENEVOLENT AND SICK FUNDS.

Mr. A. LANG. in submitting the report of the Benevo- lent Fund, thanked the members for Voir response to appeals for assistance. The Committee bad been able to give temporary assistance in 25 cases. The income, including a balance in hand at the beginning of the year was 6 3s. 3d., and the expenditure £4 151., leav- ing a balance in band of £1 Bs. 3i• There had been no eases of an exceptional character during the year. The Christmas cheer which was given helped to brighten a number of homes. Proceeding to speak of the sick fund which had been started, be said there were now 96 names on the register, and they had about £l2 in hand. It was soundly established, and be would appeal to young men to join it. The fund taught them lessons of eelf-respect, and enabled them to help one another in time of need without having recourse to charitable socie- ties. The reports were adopted.

div.head: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.
div.p: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

The election of officers was then proceeded with, with the following results : President, Rev John Yong° ; General Secretary, Mr Thomas Wallington ; Assistant Secretary, Mr. B Farrar ; Treasurer, Idr R Atkinson ; Secretary, Benevolent Fund, Mr A Lang ; Treasurer, Benevolent Fund, Mr T Hawthorn ; Absentee Visitors Secretary, Mr Mills ; Rewards, Mr Wocds and Mr Langford ; and a large general committee.
VOTES 07 THANKS. A vote of thanks was unanimously passed ti all who had assisted in the work of the Society, and the meet- ing concluded with the singing of the Doxology.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

COLLIERY FATALITY AT SUTTON' HEATH. An inquest was held before Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, at the Railway Hotel, Thatto Heath, St. Helens, on Saturday, on the body of Mark Naylor, 39 years of age, collier, ot 29, Bamber-street, who was killed in the Sutton Heath Colliery of the Sutton Heath and Lea Green Collieries Company. Mr. H. Hall. Government inspector of mines, was present ; Mr. S. Glover,.J.P., misers' agent also attended ; and Mr. James Robinson, certificated manager, represented the firm. It appeared that while Naylor was engaged in his usual working place, a large quantity of stones and dirt fell from the roof, and he was completely buried beneath the debris. John Hardman, a drawer, witnessed the fall, and imme- diately gave an alarm. Efforts were made to reQcusi Naylor. but when his body was reeovered life was ex- tinct. The evidence showed that" sprees" were being set to support the roof a: the time of the accident, and the jury in returning a verdict of' • Accidental death," recommended that certain steps should be taken to pre vent a recurrence of such an accident. FATAL WAGONETTE ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS. At St. Helens Town Hall on Tuesday, Mr. Coroner Brighouse held an inquest on the body of Henry Green, aged twenty-rune years. a labourer, of 41, Earl-street, who was knocked down and kiiled on Saturday night by a wagonette belonging to to the St. Helene and District Carriage Company, which ran over hi 4 heal.—Mr. E. W. Swift represented the Carriage Company, and Mr. J. Haslam FOl representea the relatives of deceased.—Mre. Green gave evidence of identification, and said tha: on Saturday night she and her husband left horn,. at half- past eight to go marketing. They were returning along Sharp-street:about twenty minutes pasteeleven. They were arm-in-arm en the footpath going towards Parr.. They both stepped off the footpath, when they were. suddenly knocked down by a wagonette coming tc- wards them. Her husband had had two glasses of beer. —Benjamin Edwards, or 9, Corporation-street, coachman for Dr. O'Keefe said that on Satur- day night he was in Sharp Street, and saw the steam tram and waggonette going along past one ancther, when he heard a scream, and saw the twol people under the waggonette, and the hind wheel went over the man's head.—By Mr. Goodall : The tram and wagonette were close together, and the noise of the tram would drown the noise of the waggonette.—By Mr. Swift : The driver pulled his horses right across the road in order to avoid the penple if possible —Henry Jones, the driver of the waggonette belonging to the St. Helens Carriage Company, said he was returning with feur horses from Abbey Likes Hotel, Upholland, and had twenty-six people on. When he was coming along Sharp-street he saw the man and woman step off the footpath about three or fcur yards in front of the horses. He pulled the horses across, and the frent wheel missed the man, but the hind wheel did not.—Constable Griffiths said he saw the man taken to the Providence Hospital,where he died in the entrance. The driver was perfectly sober, and had two good lights on the waggons ette.—The jury re'urned a verdict of " Accidental death," several of them giving the opinion that the foot- path was dangerous owing to the channel stones being higher than the road. They exonerated the driver from all blame.—The Coroner said he thoroughly agreed with the verdict.

div.head: NEWTON, HAYDOCIC, AND GOLBORNE BUILDING SOCIETY.
div.p: NEWTON, HAYDOCIC, AND GOLBORNE BUILDING SOCIETY.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual general meeting of this society was held in the Town Hall, Newton, on Friday evening. There was only a poor attendance of members. Mr. J. Sankey nresided, and amongst those present were Messrs. H. J. Loneton, J Croutchlev, J. Lawton, John Simpson, T. Ritchie, J Bateman, LI. The Chairman asked them to take the following annual report and balance sheet, as read, and this was agreed to.

div.head: REPORT AND BALANCE NIEET.
div.p: REPORT AND BALANCE NIEET.

" The Directors have pleasure in reporting to the members the Society's transactions for the past year, and presenting to them the annexed statement of accounts, certified by the auditors. Advances have been made this year on twelve lots of Property amounting to £4,890, and after deducting repayments the total sum outstanding on properties not in hand is £20,729 7s 51 en fifty lots. The profits for the year are £925 18s 10d, and a divieend of 41, per cent. has been declared, which will absorb £794 4s 9d, leaving £l3l 14s ld to be carried to the Contingent Account, which now stands at £2,936 10a. This is nearly 131 per cent. on the total sum outstanding on mort g ge. The directors congratulate the members on thee .etinued proiperity of the Society. A large am tint of business has been done during the year, and the°advances have been made with grett care, nearly all °f which are local ; and the steady increase of the reserve shows the sound position in which the Society stands. One property only is in the Society's hands. The directors are prepared te make advances on liberal terms on eligible treehold or leasehold properties, and in addition to the issuing of invested shares, they are pre- pared to receive deposits or leans at a fixed rate ot interest at 3 per cent., payable half-pearly, and subjec,--. tovarious terms of notice for repayment. The Society consists of 327 members, holding 1842 invested shares (paid up and partly paid up), and 2,663 mortgage shares. The Chairman said the report spoke sufficently for self • No doubt they would notice the year just rassed had been a very successful one. They had done good stroke of business, having advanced money on 12 different lots of property, each of which the directors thought was all right, and within easy retch of Newton. Out of the workings, the managers had decided to d - clare a dividend of 4i per cent., which he theueht was very good indeed. .ome people thought they should have gene a little further, but he did not think it would be a wise plan. They were carrying a nice sum to the contingent fund, and it woul Ibe there when it was wanted. He booed things would go on aril promer. It seemed to him that Building .9 cie-iea had net finiThed yet, there was something in store for them if properly worked. He did not thiek there were any erearer facili- ties for the working marl than Building Soriptiea. He concluded by moving the adoption of the report and bal- ance sheet. Mr. Thomas Jacktnn secondel, and ,ad it required no words of his ta speak in favour of the report. As one of the directors of the society, he could vouch for the sound position in which it stood. He could only reiter at whst•the chairman had said, that they had done very well this year, and he had no fear but that the business they had done was bona fide. (Hear, hear). The balance sheet was then adopted. Mr. Bateman, one of the auditore, said that everything had been carried out satisfactorily and the balance sheet showed that the Ssciety was in a sound condition. Mr. H. J. Longten said it usually happened when a eoncern was doing well, the shareholders and members were so satisfied that they did not care to attend the meetings: At the same time be thought the Directors would have been glad to meet them and hear any re- marks they had to maks. He could soinoide with the remarks that bad been made and could say that the society was in t satisfactory condition. Mr. J. Adams, secretary, also spoke and urged the members to endeavour to considerably increase the membership. The who:* of the officers of the Society were re-elected and a vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the meet- ing toa close.

Mr. Baooics : The question has nothing bdo with the passing of this resolution. Mr. PILLING : After the names I have given I think it wrong for Mr. Thornton to press this matter. I have told him the Chairman of the company.

Mr. Knowtas : Who is he? Mr. PILLING : Mr. Alderman Francomb. I believe Mr. Thornton thinks there are some connected with the company members of this Board. The only one I know of is Mr. A. Jolley. Mr. Knowles : Is he one of the directors ? (Laughter.) Mr. PILLING He is the only man in connection with the Board of Guardians who is associated with the company. Mr. HICKMAN rose to speak but the Chairman ruled him out of Order. Mr. HICKMAN : I seconded the amendment• The CHAIRMAN : Y-Ju have spoken already. Mr. HICKMAN : Alright I will bow to your ruling. Mr. WM. HOUGHTON as mover of the resolution re- plied. He said the committee was entirely unanimouc in submitting the recommendations and when he told Mr. Hickman (who was unable to be present), their de- cision, he said be entirely approved of what had been done.

Mr. HICKMAN : I shall want to make a persoNal ex- planation about that. Mr. HOUGFITON (c intineing) said it must not be thought that the committee did not take measures to know with whom they were dealing. The company was a respectable firm and there was a material differ- OLIC3 in their contract. He hoped that if the amend- ment were not withdrawn that the Board would sup- port the minutee. Mr. HICKMAN on being allowed to make a personal ex- planation said an did not object to what the committee had done, but seconded the amendment in order to as• certain the persons with whom they were dealing. Mr. Asaceorr Cannot we have the names ot all the directors? Oaly three have been given. Mr. PILLING: I have given the Chairman. The amendment en being put to the meeting was lost. Mr. KeowLes : I will put the question in this way. With whom are we trading? The lAIRMAN You have the name : The Warring- ton District Electric Light and Power Company. Mr. KNOWLES : flit is a public company there need be no secret as to the raernber3 of it.

The CHAIRMAN: The names have already been given twice in the presence of the reporters. Mr. Tunerwroe : Have all the names been given'? Mr. Omni : Mr. Miller wishes it to be distinctly understood that he did not know anyone in connection with the company when he reported on their estimate. I made some enquiries myself and so far as they went they were quite satisfactory. The company has done .work ler two local firms and it was done satisfactorily. The Board will be protected by the contract to be drawn up by the Clerk. This will protect the Board from any loss, either by the firm becoming bankrupt—(laughter) —or anything else. Mr. THORNTON : May I ask how many competitors there were for the contract ? Mr. OWEN : There were three others. Mr. THORNTON : Will you give me the firms and the amount of the contracts? Mr. OWEN : Messrs. Brigs,' and Gorham, London, £2,955 16s ; Messrs. Edmoneson's Limited, £2,929 10i; Warringtou District Electric Light and Power Company £2,436 ss; Calvert and Company, Manchester, £2,419. The estimate of Messrs. Calvert was not in accordance with specifications. On sending in a second tender their price was £2,793. Mr. Miller had since added a booster which would cost an additional £l4O to the con- tracts submitted. The CHAIRMAN : All this has already been put before the Guardians. Mr. THORNTON : I notice that the contract of Calvert and Company was lower than that of the Warrington Compaey in the first instance. Some alterations have since taken place. Why have they taken place ? Mr. MILLER : In their erdinary estimate Calvert and Company included a battery which was not in accord- ance with specification. In a subsequent estimate they quoted for a larger size and the additional cost was £370. When that sum was added to Messrs. Calvert's original estimate it exceeded that of the Warriagten Company. The CHAIRMAN : Although Calvert's estimate seemed to be lower it was not really lower. The recornmnriations of the committee were then passed and the Board rose. WA.RRINGTON RURA.L DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The minthly meeting uf this Council was held on Wednesday afternoon at the Bewaey-street Chambers. Mr. Joshua Ball presided, and there were also present— Messrs Joseph Knowles,ik Brooks,W Houghton,Johnson„ P Longton, Forshaw, 'nouns Halton, Henry Thornton with Messrs J C Suttpn (clerk), Samuel Sutton (assis- tant clerk), Dr Sepbton (medical officer), W Thompson (surveyor), and F Kerfoot (inspector).
FASHIONABLE WEDDING AT NEWTON.

There was a large gathering at St. Peter's Church, Newton, on Wednesday afterneon, on the occasion of the mat riaze of Miss Maud Mary Thorp, eldest daughter of Mr. Albert Thorp, Mere House. Newton, with Eustace F. D. Bouth, fourth son of Dr. F. W. D. Booth, Leigh. The father of the bride is a member of the firm of Messrs J. and J. ['eyes, Cotton Spinners, Leigh, and the fattier of the bridegroom is head of the firm of T. W. D. Bouth and Company, also Cotton Spinners of Lcigh. The bride was attired in a gown of ivory Duchesse satin, with court train and bodice embroidered with raised: flowers and chiffon and chenille in a design of roses and leaves. She wore an embroidered tulle veil over a wreath of orange blossom, and carried a shower bouquet, the gift of the bridegroom. Is ornaments she wore a diamond and pearl pendant, also the gift of the bridegroom. Her bridesmaids were MiS3 Gertrude Thorp, sister of the bride, Miss Eva M. Thorp, cous n, whose costumes consisted of cream silk voile with lace applique and embroidery made over cream and glee silk with fichus and sashes of chiffon and lace ; large white picture hats trimmed with , ostrich feathers and tulle. They carried shower boquets of pink roses, and lilies of the valley tied with chiffon the gift of the bridegroom. • Two of the bride- groom's nieces, Miss Muriel and Gladys Mouth acted as trainbearers and were dressed in white embroidered silk with lace insqrcions and chiffon sashes ; and large white hats. All four wore gold and pearl whips and merry-thought brooches, given by the bridegroom. The best man was Mr. Rollo F. D. Bouth. The bride was given away by Mr. L.E. Whittaker of Willow bank, Nev.ton. The service was fully choral, and as the bridal party entered the church the choir sang "The voice that breathed o'er Eden," and afterwards " 0 perfect peace." The church was boautifully and profusely decorated with white flowers, palms and foliage plants. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. R• H. M. Bouth. Rector of Elkstone, brother of the bridegroom, assisted by the Rev. J. Ryder, vicar of Newton. A. reception was afterwards held at Mere House, and Mr. and Mrs Eustace Bouth left tor Devon. shire later in the afternoon ; the bride's travelling dress being pale blue cloth trimmed with cream braid, and hat trimmed with roses and iris. Mr. A. Irwin, of Man- chester, presided at the organ in the church. There were a large number of presents of a useful and costly character, chiefly from residents of Leigh.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

A special meeting of this Board was held in the Board Room at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Mr A J Jolley presided and there were also present: Rev W H Drummond, Rev T Matthews, Dr Patterson, Mrs Clay, Mrs Edelsten, Messrs S Davies, r B Malkin, J Clarke H. Thornton, William Hickman, T H Ashcroft, A Jolley, J Billinge, H Hibbert, A Brooks, William Houghton, T Halton, G Pilling, P Cunliffe, J W Knowles, J Johnson, with 3 C Sutton (clerk), S Sut- ton (assistant clerk),C H Ward (workhouse master), and A Wright (superintendent Padgate schools). THE SALE OF POTATOES. The minutes of the Padgate Schools Committee hav- ing been read, Mr. THORNTON asked why the committee had neg- 4ected to sell a number of loads of potatoes when the price was about 12s. They had now come down to 63., and that meant a loss of £6. Mr. HOUGHTON, in reply, said the committee did not know until the last week what surplus there might be, nor did they know how the potatoes were going to keep. If there was anything the Schools Committee had lost the House Committee would gain to a corresponding extent. At any rate the mistake was not a grave one. Mr. THORNTON did not think the explanation was satisfactory, because at the last meeting at Padgate Mr. Hibbert sain the price was 11s. or 121. Mr. HIBBERT : I said I would find a customer who would give that. The CHAIRMAN : At the worst it is only an error of judgment. Mr. PILLING : There cannot be a loss of £6, because the house will gain £4. The minutes were confirmed. THE T'ADGATE SCHOOLS BAND. The SUPERINTENDENT of Padgate Schools reported the receipt of an application for the schools band to play in the Park. It was decided to accede to the applicstian. Mr. HICKMAN : Does the hand receive any remunera- tion? Mr. THORNTON: Yes; it goes to the band fund. At a later stage of the meeting Mr. HICKMAN stated that the band might be allowed to go out oftener than had been the case in the past. GIFTS. The SUPERINIENDENT reported presents of papers from Mr. Thornton and Air. Price ; and Mr. Ward (Work- house Master) acknowledged a parcel of papers from Mr. Wright, of the Royal Court Hotel. THE HEATING OF THE NEW INFIRMARY. The CLERK reported the result of his interview in company with Mr. Owen with Messrs. Killick and Coch- rane, of Liverpoel, with reference to their contract fee the heating of the new Infirmary. The firm reduced it to £1,750. Mr. THORNTON said he was of opinion that if the Board had held them to their original contract they would have done better. The CLERK said there was not the slightest doubt that a great increase had taken place in the price of materials since the first contract was submitted. THE YEAR BOOK. The Rev. W. H. Dnummoen asked bow soon the Guardians were to have the inlet to the Guardians Year Book which was promised some time ago. It was most important that they should have a properly prepared statistical statement. The CLERK said a number of things had interfered with them in Ihe preparatiom of the book. He believed it would be in their hands in the course of the week. ELECTRIC LIGHT FOR THE NEW INFIRMARY. THE DIRECTORS OF A WARRINGTON COMPANY. WARM DISCUSSION. Messrs. William Owen (architect) and Miller (electri- cal engineer) were is attendance at the request of the Infirmary Committee to answer questions that might be put by the Board as to the lighting of the new infirmary at the Workhouse by electricity. The following extracts from the minutes of the In- fluttery Committee and estimates of expenditure were supplied to the Board in printed form :—" After reciting reading of and discussion upon report by Mr. Thomas L. Miller, RE., of Liverpool, Mr. Miller being present and after going frilly through the report with Mr. Miller, he was requested to supplement it with another report going into the question of sufficiency of the lighting prepeeed ; of batteries and motor ; of running expenses; and boilers ; and also the advisability of omitting, or using, gas pipes and gas fittings in the new infirmary if thteelectriclighting is introduced. The supplementary re- port of Mr. Miller of 18th May was fully considered,when it was decided that the reports of Mr. Miller be adopted and that it is unnecessary to fix gaspipes. " The following figures showing the proposed expenditure for heating and het water service, fire hydrants, the supply of Appleton water for beilers,and wiring and plint for electric lighting of Infirmary. and Workhouse buildings, and meter for laundry machinery wer- read : —Estimates from contractors : Killick and Cochrane, heating and het water, £1,750 (accepted) ; Warrington District Electric Light and Power Co:, wiring, plant and motor, with boester. £2,778 ; Merry weather and Co., water pipes and hydrants, £6B 18s 81; Warrington Cor- peration, main for Appleton water, £95 ; total, £2,941 184 Bd. Approximate estimates, £2,775; or a grand total of £7,466 18s Bd. It was resolved that the amount of £7,468 18s 8d be recommended for acceptance, and that the amount should be put before the Local Government Board for approval, and the necessary steps taken to ob- tain a loan for the carrying out of the work. The ac- ceptance of Mr. Houghton's resolution as Chairman of the Infirmary Committee will therefore make necessary a further loan of about £7,000. The Clerk is of opinion the laying out of the grounds and the furnishing of the Infirmary may be provided for out of the Union's 6d. rate. Contracts already accepted :—Mr C W Daven- port, buildings. £23,266 13s ; Messrs. Killick and Cochrane, heating, Sec., £1,750 ; total, £25,016 13s. Al- ready borrowed, £25,000 ; probable additional loan, £7,000." Mr. THORNTON said he would like to know who were connected with the Warrington District Electric Light and Power Company. The CHAIRMAN : It is a recognised firm in the town who are quite competent to carry out the work. Mr WILLIAM Hooonion : It is the same firm that lighted the exhibition. Mr. PILLING said ho believed the managing chairman of the company was Alderman Francomb. Mr. Alfred Jolley was a director, and Dr. Cannel!, he believed, was else interested in the company. The CHAIRMAN said he didn't know, as a matter of fact, who were connected with the firm. Mr. ASHCROFT : It seems as if they are in contpany with the Corporation. (Laughter). Mr. PILLING said Mr. Cunnah, the architect, was con- nected with the company, and other notable people like Mr. John Crosfield and Lord Winmarleigh. (Laughter). Mr. WILLIAM HOUGHTON (chairman of the Infirmary Committee) then moved " That the minutes of the In- firmary Committee be approved and their several recom- mendations adopted ; that the plans as prepared by Messrs. Owen be approved and submitted to the Local Government Board; that an erder by that Board enabling the Guardians to borrow £7,000, or such sum as may be required for completion of the Infirmary and pay- ment of architects' fees be applied for, and that the Clerk be autherised to apply to the Public Works Loan Board for such further loan and to take such steps as he may deem advisable thereon and otherwise in relation to this resolution." He said the committee had given a patient and searching inquiry into the details of the matter, and in making the recommendations they felt confident they were acting on safe and sure grounds. He did not: tnink there could be any difference of opinion as to the special merits of electric lighting aver gas lighting. Mr. GEORGE PILLING seconded the resolution. He felt confident that the installation of electric light would make their new infirmary still more complete. Mr. H. THORNTON said he would like to ask Mr. Miller the electrical engineer, if he had a prospectus or could give any information as to the Warrington District Elec- tric Light and Power Company. The CHAIRMAN: The names of the directors have already been given. Mr. H. THORNTON: That doesn't prevent us from making inquiries airs to the prospectus of the Company. The CHAIRMAN: I think the preper thing is to apply to the secretary of the company for information of that kind.

Mr. FILLING: The firm has done any amount of work in the district. Mr. A. JOLLEY : Mr. Thornton only need go to Cros- fields to see what work has been done by the com- pany. The CHAIRMAN: I don't see that that matter affects us this morning. Mr HICKMAN : I should like to ask Mr. Miller if he thinks it is unnecessary that the gas pipes should be put in?

The CHAIRMAN: That information he has already given in a printed report. He said "No.' Mr. CLARKE : I think it would be useless to put gas fittings in when we have decided upon electric light. Mr. THORNTON : I thought Mr. Miller was here to answer any questions. The Chairmaa seems to Ise answering all the questions asked. Mr. A. J. JOLLIT : I don't wish it to be thought that I am trying to stifle discussion. The Rev. W. H. DRUMMOND thought that before they accepted a large contract involving several thousands of pounds any member of the Board had a perfect right to ask a quegtion in order to satisfy himself whether the company was of sufficient commercial imprrtance to carry out the contract and not break down in the middle. Personally he did not know anything about this company. He did not know whether it had been formed three weeks or three years. Mr. WILLIAM HOUGHTON in answer to the question put by Mr. Hickman said Mr. Miller's report contained a paragraph on that subject which ran as follows : " There is no need to make provision for gas lighting." Mr. KaTowurs : Is Mr. Miller a skilled !gentleman on electric lighting ? Mr. WILLIAM HOUGHTON : He is an electrical engineer employed by the Board to advise on this matter.
