div.head: AN EARLESTOWN SIANS LEAP FROM
div.p: AN EARLESTOWN SIANS LEAP FROM
A. RAILWAY BRIDGE.
ATTEMPTED SUICIDE.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednes- day, before Mr. C. Morris (in the chair) and Mr. Frost, Charles Nelling, a young man who appeared with his arm in splints, and walked vritla a limp, was charged with attempting to commit suicide by jumping from a railway bridge at Burtonwood on June sth. R3bart Foster, carter, Berry-lane, Sutton, said he was in Broad-lane, Burtonwo3d, at eight o'clock on the the morning of the date mentiomed, and when crossing the railway bridge, saw the prisoner coming in the opposite direction. Shortly anerwards witness had to stop, and turning round saw the prisoner put his hat on the bridge and jump over. Witness ran back to the bridge and saw prisoner lying on the ground. He (witness) shouted to several people,and then went down on the line. Prisoner seemed t 3 have fallen on his side and had broken the wrist of his left hand. A train was passing at the time he jumped over the bridge. He asked prisoner what he had done it for, and he replied, "Not much."

P.C. Bateman said he received inform &en, and pro ceeded to the railway, whore he saw prisoner lyiag on his back. He asked him what was to du, but received no reply. He examined him, an/ found thst be was badly injured. He obtained a stretcher, and with assis:- ance took him to the Provid?nce Hospital in S. Helens. That morning he load charged him with attempting to commit suicide. He replied " I must have been mad with drink. If they will only forgive me, I will be a better man." _ . . . _ .

The Police Buperlnt3ndent said the prisoner had bean Living in Earlestown,and working at the Vulcan Foundry. Hs had been drinking heavily. His step-tather, Charles Coombe, of Davonport, was pre3eat, and was willing to tak3 care of him.
Prisoner was accordingly discharged.

div.head: "AND IN THE EARTH BENEATH."
div.p: "AND IN THE EARTH BENEATH."

One would think, that with the numerous 'buses, trams, cabs, and motor-cars, we had sufficient means for transit from one point of our metropolis to another. But this ld not so. No more traffic can reasonably be put on the already overcrowded streets, and the eitbject of aerial flight has not been, up to now, a success, so transit through tae earth was the only means left to us. Engineers have been hard at work, and are con- structing a railroad that will carry us quickly and at a small Cost through the city.. . . _

_ Where hind is cheap the work of laying down rails involves a comparatively small expenditure ; where the line runs through the most valuable property in the world, as the city of London un- questionably ia, millions must be sunk in order to obtain the right of mining through or beneath it. Even then the work is only half finished. Subsid- ences in the soil may occur; water mains may .oe broken; sewer tunnels may go away; and even when the works have for years been completed some flaw may be discovered. As an example of some of the dangers, take the alarming discovery made the other day in reference to the Smithfield Market. The Metropolitan Rail- way tans underneath the whole of this ponderous structure. Iron girders were put up when the line was constructed thirty years ago, but the other day the engineering detectives discovered something in the nick of time ; had they found it three weeks later a portion of the City of London would have fallen below the earth. A railway station haa been built right below one of the most ancient churches in the City, Without distuibing the architecture of the edifice itself, the ceurch of St. Mary Wooluoth, the wnola of the massive foundations of the church were removed, the earth was removed to the extent of seventy feet, and there, while millions of people were mov- ing every week in the thoroughfares overhead, the workman bored his way at the rata of eighteen feet day,until he had finished a line which enabled the I City merchant to do a thirty minutes journey in three minutes. This line was the City and South London Exten- sion, and the station Lombard-street station. Every mile of the railway cost £600,000. Each of the three lines which have been built in recent years took several years to construct. Not one of the myriads of people who hurried their way through the streets of the city knew what was going on. All that the pedestrian passing along the street could see was a number of tall hoardings inclosing a few square yards at the junction of the streets,ana above tue wooden structure the projecting pulleys and chains of huge cranes. The boring is done by a great instrument called a shield. it is driven forward by compressed air. The ponderous implement moves slowly, and were it not for the great clods of clay that come tumbling into the tunnel as the searp edge pierces it, one would hardly be conscious of the movement. IV hen it stops the miners with pick and chisel attack the clay in front. Others swing the iron segments of the tunnel into the position j ust cleared by the shield. In a few hours more the men at the clay workings make sufficient clearance to enable the shield to be driven forward another twenty inches. The Wt. Gin, tunnel advances eighteen feet every twenty-tour hours, the work proceeding night and day. curiously enough, the church of St. Mary Wool- moth stands now on stronger supports than it ever had dune before. The space below the church was being,dug out to a depth of twenty teat where the top floor level of the lifts was built together with the booking office. Then the shaft of oblon2 seg- mental shape, 241 t. by 731 t. inside, descended from this point to a depth of eighty feet to the railway station below. From the level of the church floor to the station lies a depth of over one hundred lest and down this five lilts are continually working under the church. It was a solicitor who first hit upon the idea of effecting transit below the level of tne streets. He worked at the subject from 1837, the year when the queen came to the thorne. ltie first Act of Parlia- ment on the subject was passed in 1854, and the initial section of the line was opened for the con- venience of the public in 1863. Thirty years after the passage of tee Act the inner circle of railways was completed. It is over thirteen miles in length and constitutes a subterranean circle around London:

Thew are twenty-seven stations built upon it at about half-a-mile apart. it is hard to distinguish one from the other,since the smoky atmosphere has begramed even the white enamelled letters which mark the name of the station. But smoke and underground railway seems to be inseparable. Even where the train is driven by electricity, medical authorities have discovered there is a greater danger than smoke. All the means of venti- lation are supplied by the passing of the engines below; and in the case of a breakdown a medical journal has pointed out that the passengers would be suffocated. the idea, however, has been ridiculed by the electrical engineers.
ANOTHER THUNDERSTORM. MAN KILLED AND DWELLING HOUSES DESTROYED. SIX PERSONS BURIED IN THE RUINS.

Nenagh telegram reports that a terrific thunder- storm broke over that district on Wednesday evening. The lightning, which was of a startling vividnesi,cauaed the deaths of cattle in four places round the town,while a man named Ryan, engaged on farmwork, was killed instantly. The lightning also struck a dwelling-house, dismantling it. Six persons were buried beneath the debris, and their fate was unknown at the time of tele- graphing, but a rescue party was endeavouring to reach them.

OUTBREAK OF FEVER AT THE HAGUE, PEACE DELEGATES AFFECTED. THE HAGUE. THURSDAY.

A local fever of a malarious caaractor, but very mild in its effect, is prevalent here. It is attributed to emanations from numerous canals into which the sevrage of the city runs. Some members of the Peace Couien- ence are affected.

Mr. E. S. Cooke, 8.A., of Pembroke College, Oxford, and now headmaster of the Pupil Teachers' Central Classes, Bournemouth, has been appointed headmaster of St. Paul's Day Schools, vice Mr. D. W. Finney. who will resign his duties at the end of the financial year, i.e September 30th. Mr. Coke comes with the very highest qualifications for the post. There were over 180 applications. SPIRITUALISM.

The Sunday evening meeting of this society was addresed by Mr. J Moorey, of Manchester, his sub- ject being "Sowing and reaping,"in dealing with which he pointed out the inevitable nature of the law of consequences, and the manner in which oor thoughts, our words and our actions were as so many seeds which would inevitably spring up and bear fruit affecting ourselves and those by whom we were surrounded. M this as well as the after- noon meeting Mr. Moovey gave a number of clair- voyant delineations. LORD JOHN SANG-IMS AND SONS' CIRCUS AT W ARRING TON.

This popular circus paid a visit to Warrington on Tuesday. At one o'clock there was a lengthy and attractive procession through the principal streets of the town, and, needless to say, it was witnessed by thousands of people. In the afternoon, on the the Blue Coat school field, off Winwick-road, a per- formance of a very meritorious character was given, but the audience was very small. The elephants are particularly clever, and they went through their part of the programme in a manner which left nothing to be desired. Excellent music was pre- vided by the band. Another performance was given in the evening. SHOCKING ACCIDTINT TO A WARRINGTON MAN.

Late on Wednesday evening, Richard Gurney,who is in the employ of Mr. John Maginn, furniture remover, Warrington, met with a shocking accident in the neighbourhood of Minshull Vernon. He was proceeding with en empty furniture van, to which three horses were attached, from Warrington to Whitchurcb, and as he was passing the house of Mr. F. Davies, of Minshull Vernon,he fell from the van on which he was riding, and it is supposed that before the vehicle could be pulled up one of the wheels passed over his head. Several gentlemen front Crewe, who were cycling, happened to be passing at the time and went to Gurney's assist- ance. They found that he was very badly injured and unconscious. A message was dispatched on a bicycle to Crewe for medical assistance, and Dr. Lowe was speedily in attendance. By his direction the man was conveyed to an adjoining inn, where he now lies in a critical condition, having a severe scalp wound and being much bruised about the body.

PLAYING CHESS, DRAUGHTS, AND WHIST SIM- ULTANEOUSLY.—At the Ladies' Chess Club, Regent- street, London, last week. Mr. Pillsbury repeated the wonderful feat of playing against ten players eight games of chess and two games of draughts, while engaging in a rubber of whist. The methods of the chessmaster's play were as remarkable as the triple game itself. The moves made by each of his opponents at chess and draughts, seated in a differ- ent part of the ro3m, were called out aloud, and as often as not, Mr. Pillsbury would utter his reply without halting in his card play or stopping in his deal. He never kept his partners waiting for any appreciable time.
